nodes.name: Linear hyperbolic relaxation system (zero relaxation Cauchy problem)
nodes.statement: This work is concerned with the Cauchy problems for first-order linear hyperbolic relaxation systems with stiff source terms in several spatial variables: \begin{equation} \pd{U}{t} + \sum_{j = 1}^d A_j \pd{U}{x_j} = \frac{1}{\varepsilon} Q U, \quad U(0, x, \varepsilon^{-1}) = U_0(x), \end{equation} where the relaxation time $\varepsilon > 0$ is a small parameter, $U$ is the unknown $n$-vector function of $(t, x, \eta) = (t, x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_d, \eta) \in [0, +\infty) \times \mathbb{R}^d \times [0, +\infty)$ with $\eta = \varepsilon^{-1}$, and the matrices $Q \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ and $A_j \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ with $j = 1, 2, \ldots, d$ are constant matrices.
definiendum: first-order linear hyperbolic relaxation systems with stiff source terms
nodes.statement_short: The Cauchy problem $U_t+\sum_j A_j U_{x_j}=\varepsilon^{-1}QU$ with constant matrices and relaxation time $\varepsilon$, $\eta=\varepsilon^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Quasi-stability and uniform quasi-stability
nodes.statement: A matrix $M \in \mathbb{C}^{n \times n}$ is called \textit{quasi-stable} if \begin{displaymath} \sup_{t \ge 0} \norm{e^{M t}} < + \infty. \end{displaymath} A set of matrices $\mathcal{F} \subset \mathbb{C}^{n \times n}$ is called \textit{uniformly quasi-stable} if \begin{displaymath} \sup_{M \in \mathcal{F}} \sup_{t \ge 0} \norm{e^{M t}} < + \infty. \end{displaymath}
nodes.statement_short: A matrix is quasi-stable if $e^{Mt}$ is bounded for $t\ge0$; a set is uniformly quasi-stable if the bound is uniform.

nodes.name: Characterization of quasi-stability (Kreiss-Lorenz)
nodes.statement: For any $M \in \mathbb{C}^{n \times n}$, the following two conditions are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item The matrix $M$ is quasi-stable. \item All eigenvalues $\lambda$ of the matrix $M$ have a real part $\Re(\lambda) \le 0$. Furthermore, if $J_r$ is a Jordan block of the Jordan matrix $J = S M S^{-1}$, corresponding to an eigenvalue $\lambda_r$ of the matrix $M$ with $\Re(\lambda_r) = 0$, then $J_r$ has dimension $1 \times 1$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: A matrix is quasi-stable iff its eigenvalues have nonpositive real parts and those on the imaginary axis are semi-simple.
assumptions: $M \in \mathbb{C}^{n \times n}$
conclusions: the following two conditions are equivalent.
equivalent_conditions: All eigenvalues $\lambda$ of the matrix $M$ have a real part $\Re(\lambda) \le 0$.
nodes.label: lemma:QS_character

conclusions: The following four conditions are equivalent.

nodes.name: Model Cauchy problem with source term
nodes.statement: To elucidate an essential technique used in our proof and the motivation behind improving the resolvent estimates in the Kreiss matrix theorem, let us consider the following Cauchy problem: \begin{equation} \pd{u}{t} = \mathcal{A} u + f(t, x), \quad u(0, x) = 0, \end{equation} where $u$ is the unknown $n$-vector function of $(t, x) = (t, x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_d) \in [0, +\infty) \times \mathbb{R}^d$, the source term $f$ is an $n$-vector function of $(t, x)$, the differential operator $\mathcal{A}$ is defined by $(\mathcal{A} v)^{\wedge}(\xi) := A(\xi) \hat{v}(\xi)$, where $\hat{v}$ is the Fourier transform of an $n$-vector function $v$ defined on $\mathbb{R}^d$, and the symbol of $\mathcal{A}$, denoted as $A(\xi)$, is an $n \times n$-matrix function of $\xi \in \mathbb{R}^d$.
nodes.statement_short: Auxiliary Cauchy problem $u_t=\mathcal{A}u+f$, $u(0)=0$, with Fourier symbol $A(\xi)$ of the operator $\mathcal{A}$.

nodes.statement: \pd{u}{t} = \mathcal{A} u + f(t, x), \quad u(0, x) = 0,

nodes.name: Kreiss resolvent bound for well-posed Cauchy problems
nodes.statement: Under the assumption of well-posedness \cite{kreiss_initial-boundary_2004} of \cref{eq:cauchy}, the Kreiss matrix theorem implies the existence of constants $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and $K > 0$ independent of $\xi$ such that the following resolvent estimate holds: \begin{equation} \|{(z I - A(\xi))^{-1}}\| \le \frac{K}{\Re(z) - \alpha}, \end{equation} for each $z \in \mathbb{C}$ whose real part satisfies $\Re(z) > \alpha$.
nodes.statement_short: Well-posedness plus the Kreiss matrix theorem give $\|(zI-A(\xi))^{-1}\|\le K/(\Re z-\alpha)$.
assumptions: Under the assumption of well-posedness \cite{kreiss_initial-boundary_2004} of \cref{eq:cauchy}
conclusions: the following resolvent estimate holds:

nodes.name: Kreiss resolvent bound
nodes.statement: \|{(z I - A(\xi))^{-1}}\| \le \frac{K}{\Re(z) - \alpha},
nodes.label: eq:cauchy_KMTbound

nodes.name: Kreiss resolvent bound is too rough
nodes.statement: By applying the Fourier transform and the Laplace transform to both sides of \cref{eq:cauchy}, one can derive the following equation: \begin{displaymath} z \tilde{u}(z, \xi) = A(\xi) \tilde{u}(z, \xi) + \tilde{f}(z, \xi), \end{displaymath} under some appropriate assumptions on the functions $A(\xi)$ and $f(t, x)$. Here, $\tilde{u}(z, \xi)$ is the Laplace transform with respect to the variable $t$ of the Fourier transform $\hat{u}(t, \xi)$ of the function $u(t, x)$. Therefore, it follows that $\tilde{u}(z, \xi) = (z I - A(\xi))^{-1} \tilde{f}(z, \xi)$. The inverse Laplace transform of $\tilde{u}(z, \xi)$ is determined by \begin{displaymath} \hat{u}(t, \xi) = \frac{1}{2 \pi i} \int_{\gamma - i \infty}^{\gamma + i \infty} e^{z t} (z I - A(\xi))^{-1} \tilde{f}(z, \xi) \,\mathrm{d} z, \end{displaymath} where $\gamma$ is a real number such that the contour line lies in the region of convergence of $\tilde{u}(z, \xi)$ for each $\xi \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and the integral is understood in the sense of the principal value. One may estimate $\hat{u}(t, \xi)$ as \begin{displaymath} \|{\hat{u}(t, \xi)}\| \le \frac{e^{\gamma t}}{2 \pi} \int_{- \infty}^{+ \infty} \|{(z I - A(\xi))^{-1}}\| \cdot \|{\tilde{f}(z, \xi)}\| \,\mathrm{d} y, \end{displaymath} where $z = \gamma + i y$. The Kreiss matrix theorem provides the resolvents with an upper bound, as given in \cref{eq:cauchy_KMTbound}, which depends only on the real part of $z$. However, this bound is too rough, as for fixed $\xi$ and $\gamma$, it holds that $\|{(z I - A(\xi))^{-1}}\| = \mathcal{O}(|y|^{-1})$ as $|y| \rightarrow + \infty$, while \cref{eq:cauchy_KMTbound} cannot capture the decay of the resolvents. To obtain a more accurate upper bound for $\hat{u}(t, \xi)$, we require sharper resolvent estimates.
nodes.statement_short: Via Fourier-Laplace transform the solution is a contour integral of the resolvent; Kreiss's bound misses the $O(|y|^{-1})$ decay, motivating sharper estimates.

nodes.name: Open right-half complex plane
nodes.statement: Henceforth, we denote the open right-half complex plane as \begin{displaymath} \mathbb{H} = \left\{ z \in \mathbb{C} \,\big|\, \Re(z) > 0 \right\}.

nodes.name: Measurement of uniform quasi-stability K(M)
nodes.statement: For a matrix $M \in \mathbb{C}^{n \times n}$, the spectrum of $M$ is denoted as $\sigma(M)$, and we define a new measurement of uniform quasi-stability as: \begin{displaymath} \mathcal{K}(M) := \sup_{z \in \mathbb{H}} \frac{\norm{(z I - M)^{-1}}} {\max_{\lambda \in \sigma(M) \setminus \mathbb{H}} |z - \lambda|^{-1}}. \end{displaymath} When $\sigma(M)$ is a subset of the half-plane $\mathbb{H}$, we set $\mathcal{K}(M) := + \infty$.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{K}(M)$ is the sup over $\Re z>0$ of the resolvent norm relative to the inverse distance to the non-right-half-plane spectrum.

nodes.name: Improved resolvent estimate in the Kreiss matrix theorem
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a set of matrices in $\mathbb{C}^{n \times n}$. The matrix set $\mathcal{F}$ is uniformly quasi-stable if and only if \begin{equation} \sup_{M \in \mathcal{F}} \mathcal{K}(M) < + \infty. \end{equation} In this case, there exists a positive constant $K$ such that \begin{equation} \norm{(z I - M)^{-1}} \le K \max_{\lambda \in \sigma(M)} |z - \lambda|^{-1}, \end{equation} for each $M \in \mathcal{F}$ and $z \in \mathbb{H}$.
nodes.statement_short: A matrix set is uniformly quasi-stable iff $\sup\mathcal{K}(M)<\infty$; then the resolvent is bounded by $K$ times the inverse distance to the spectrum.
assumptions: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a set of matrices in $\mathbb{C}^{n \times n}$.
conclusions: The matrix set $\mathcal{F}$ is uniformly quasi-stable if and only if

nodes.name: Related work on improving resolvent estimates
nodes.statement: Numerous studies have been dedicated to improving the uniform upper bounds of the semigroups under Kreiss's resolvent condition, as investigated in \cite{leveque_resolvent_1984,van_linear_1993}. The focus of \Cref{thm:IKMT} is on the converse, i.e., improving the resolvent estimates for a uniformly quasi-stable matrix set. Several attempts have been made in this direction. For instance, J. Miller \cite{miller_resolvent_1968} estimated the resolvents along specific contours in the left-half complex plane by categorizing the spectrum of each matrix. R. Zarouf \cite{zarouf_sharpening_2009} refined the resolvent estimates for power-bounded matrices using Bernstein-type inequalities for rational functions. Detailed discussions of these results and their relations to \Cref{thm:IKMT} are presented in \Cref{app:kreiss}.
nodes.statement_short: Prior work improved semigroup bounds under the resolvent condition; Theorem 2 goes the converse way, related to Miller and Zarouf.

nodes.name: Zero is a semi-simple eigenvalue of Q
nodes.statement: A basic assumption of Yong's stability conditions is that zero is a semi-simple eigenvalue of the matrix $Q$, i.e., there exists an invertible $n \times n$ matrix $P$ and an invertible $r \times r$ matrix $B$ such that \begin{equation} P Q P^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & B \end{pmatrix}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $Q$ is similar to $\mathrm{diag}(0,B)$ with $B$ invertible.

nodes.name: Block form of Q
nodes.statement: P Q P^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & B \end{pmatrix}.
nodes.label: eq:Yong1_PQPinv

nodes.name: Yong's stability conditions
nodes.statement: We say that \cref{eq} satisfies \textit{Yong's first stability condition} if the following requirements hold: \begin{enumerate}[label={(\roman{enumi})}] \item All the eigenvalues of the matrix $B$ in \cref{eq:Yong1_PQPinv} have negative real parts; \item \Cref{eq} is \textit{symmetrizable hyperbolic}, i.e., there exists a positive definite Hermitian matrix $A_0$ such that $A_0 A_j = A_j^* A_0$ for each $j = 1, 2, \ldots, d$; \item The hyperbolic and source terms satisfies \begin{displaymath} A_0 Q + Q^* A_0 \le 0. \end{displaymath} \end{enumerate} We say that \cref{eq} satisfies \textit{Yong's second stability condition} if it satisfies the requirements \ref{cond:Yong1}, \ref{cond:Yong2}, and \begin{enumerate}[start=3,label={(\roman{enumi})$^\prime$}] \item The hyperbolic and source terms are coupled in the sense that \begin{displaymath} A_0 Q + Q^* A_0 \le - P^* \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & I_r \end{pmatrix} P. \end{displaymath} \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Yong's first condition: $B$ stable, a symmetrizer $A_0$ for all $A_j$, and $A_0Q+Q^*A_0\le0$; the second strengthens the coupling condition.

nodes.name: Non-oscillation assumption
nodes.statement: \Cref{cond:Yong1} is equivalent to the statement that the matrix $Q$ is quasi-stable and has no purely imaginary eigenvalues different from zero, which is just the \textit{non-oscillation assumption} \cite{Yong_basic_2002}. Under the basic assumption presented in \cref{eq:Yong1_PQPinv}, \Cref{cond:Yong3s} implies \Cref{cond:Yong1} as shown in \cite[Lemma 2.1]{Yong_singular_1999}.
nodes.statement_short: Condition (i) is the non-oscillation assumption; (iii)' implies (i).
nodes.label: rmk:yong->noa

nodes.name: Yong's condition extends symmetrizable hyperbolicity
nodes.statement: Symmetrizable hyperbolicity is an easily verifiable condition for the following first-order partial differential equations with non-stiff source terms: \begin{equation} \pd{U}{t} + \sum_{j = 1}^d A_j \pd{U}{x_j} = Q U. \end{equation} However, it is not the weakest condition to ensure the well-posedness of \cref{eq:1st} as pointed out in \cite{kreiss_initial-boundary_2004}. \Cref{cond:Yong2,cond:Yong3w} in Yong's first stability condition can be seen as a natural extension of symmetrizable hyperbolicity in the case of hyperbolic relaxation systems presented in \cref{eq}.
nodes.statement_short: Conditions (ii),(iii) extend symmetrizable hyperbolicity of non-stiff first-order systems to relaxation systems.
nodes.label: rmk:relation_yong

nodes.name: First-order system with non-stiff source
nodes.statement: \pd{U}{t} + \sum_{j = 1}^d A_j \pd{U}{x_j} = Q U.
nodes.label: eq:1st

nodes.name: Stiff well-posedness
nodes.statement: We say that \cref{eq} satisfies the condition of \textit{stiff well-posedness} or it is \textit{stiffly well-posed} if the matrix set, \begin{displaymath} \mathcal{F}_0 := \left\{ H(\xi, \eta) \,\big|\, \xi \in \mathbb{R}^d, \eta \ge 0 \right\}, \end{displaymath} is uniformly quasi-stable, where \begin{equation} H = H(\xi, \eta) := \eta Q - i \sum_{j = 1}^d \xi_j A_j. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: System (1) is stiffly well-posed if $\{\eta Q - i\sum_j\xi_jA_j\}$ is uniformly quasi-stable over $\xi\in\mathbb{R}^d$, $\eta\ge0$.
nodes.label: def:stiff_well_posedness

nodes.name: Symbol H(xi, eta)

nodes.name: Strong hyperbolicity
nodes.statement: Parallel to the discussions in \Cref{rmk:relation_yong}, stiff well-posedness can be regarded as a natural extension of strong hyperbolicity \cite{kreiss_initial-boundary_2004} within the context of hyperbolic relaxation systems. We say that \cref{eq:1st} is \textit{strongly hyperbolic} if the matrix set, \begin{displaymath} \mathcal{F}_{00} := \left\{ H(\xi, 0) \,\big|\, \xi \in \mathbb{R}^d \right\}, \end{displaymath} is uniformly quasi-stable, where $H(\xi, \eta)$ is defined by \cref{eq:H}. According to \cite{kreiss_initial-boundary_2004}, strong hyperbolicity is equivalent to the well-posedness of \cref{eq:1st}.
nodes.statement_short: System (7) is strongly hyperbolic if $\{H(\xi,0)\}$ is uniformly quasi-stable.

nodes.name: Strong hyperbolicity is equivalent to well-posedness
nodes.statement: According to \cite{kreiss_initial-boundary_2004}, strong hyperbolicity is equivalent to the well-posedness of \cref{eq:1st}.
conclusions: strong hyperbolicity is equivalent to the well-posedness of \cref{eq:1st}.

nodes.name: Stiff well-posedness is the minimal stability requirement
nodes.statement: The condition of stiff well-posedness is the most minimal stability requirement to ensure the well-posedness of \cref{eq} in the asymptotic limit. it is equivalent to the $L^2$ boundedness of solutions in the asymptotic limit for arbitrary $L^2$ initial values in some sense, as shown by the following proposition.

nodes.name: Slow and fast variables
nodes.statement: Under the condition of stiff well-posedness, the matrix $Q$ is quasi-stable, and thus, zero is a semi-simple eigenvalue of $Q$, as indicated in the basic assumption in \cref{eq:Yong1_PQPinv}. At this point, one can consider the following equation concerning the unknown function $P U$: \begin{displaymath} \pd{(P U)}{t} + \sum_{j = 1}^d P A_j P^{-1} \cdot \pd{(P U)}{x_j} = \frac{1}{\varepsilon} P Q P^{-1} \cdot P U, \end{displaymath} and the symmetrizer $A_0$ can be substituted by $P A_0 P^{-1}$. Therefore, henceforth, when assuming the quasi-stability of the matrix $Q$, we consider the form of $Q$ to be \begin{displaymath} Q = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & B \end{pmatrix}, \end{displaymath} without loss of generality. Correspondingly, the matrices $A_j$ and $H$, and the vector $U$, can be expressed in block form as follows: \begin{displaymath} A_j = \begin{pmatrix} A_{j,11} & A_{j,12} \\ A_{j,21} & A_{j,22} \end{pmatrix}, \quad H = \begin{pmatrix} H_{11} & H_{12} \\ H_{21} & H_{22} \end{pmatrix}, \quad U = \begin{pmatrix} u \\ v \end{pmatrix}, \end{displaymath} where $u$ and $v$ represent \textit{slow variables} and \textit{fast variables}, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: WLOG $Q=\mathrm{diag}(0,B)$; block-decompose $A_j$, $H$, $U=(u,v)$ with $u$ slow and $v$ fast variables.

nodes.name: Stiff well-posedness versus Yong's first condition via the Kreiss matrix theorem
nodes.statement: The relation between stiff well-posedness and \Cref{cond:Yong2,cond:Yong3w} in Yong's first stability condition, as well as the relation between strong hyperbolicity and symmetrizable hyperbolicity, can be elucidated from the perspective of the Kreiss matrix theorem presented in \Cref{thm:KMT}. Let us consider the former as an example. According to \Cref{thm:KMT}, stiff well-posedness is equivalent to the existence of a positive constant $K_4$ such that for each $\xi \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and $\eta \ge 0$, there exists a Hermitian matrix $A_0 = A_0(\xi, \eta)$ such that \begin{equation} K_4^{-1} I \le A_0(\xi, \eta) \le K_4 I, \quad A_0(\xi, \eta) H(\xi, \eta) + H(\xi, \eta)^* A_0(\xi, \eta) \le 0. \end{equation} From \Cref{cond:Yong2,cond:Yong3w}, one can deduce the existence of a positive definite Hermitian matrix $A_0$ such that \begin{equation} A_0 H(\xi, \eta) + H(\xi, \eta)^* A_0 \le 0, \end{equation} for each $\xi \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and $\eta \ge 0$. Conversely, if \cref{eq:yong_SPD} holds for each $\xi \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and $\eta \ge 0$, \Cref{cond:Yong2,cond:Yong3w} also hold by taking $(\xi, \eta) = (0, 1), (\pm e_j, 0)$ with $j = 1, 2, \ldots, d$. Therefore, Yong's first stability condition without the non-oscillation assumption corresponds to the case when the Hermitian matrix $A_0(\xi, \eta)$ in \cref{eq:SWP_SPD} is independent of $\xi$ and $\eta$. In this case, it can be shown that $A_0$ is a block diagonal matrix \cite[Lemma 2.1]{Yong_singular_1999}, leading effortlessly to the uniform quasi-stability of the following two matrix sets: \begin{gather} \mathcal{F}_1 := \left\{ H_{11}(\xi, 0) \,\big|\, \xi \in \mathbb{R}^d \right\}, \\ \mathcal{F}_2 := \left\{ H_{22}(\xi, \eta) \,\big|\, \xi \in \mathbb{R}^d, \eta \ge 0 \right\}, \end{gather} where the former aligns with the conclusion in \Cref{lemma:UQS_of_F1}, ensuring the strong hyperbolicity of reduced systems presented in \cref{eq:reduced}, and the latter facilitates the estimation of a crucial term defined in \cref{eq:key_term} in the proof of our main result. However, it is important to note that the only assumption for \cref{eq} in this paper to establish asymptotic convergence of slow variables is stiff well-posedness, demanding additional efforts for the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Via the Kreiss matrix theorem, Yong's first condition without non-oscillation is stiff well-posedness with a constant symmetrizer, giving uniform quasi-stability of $\mathcal{F}_1,\mathcal{F}_2$.
nodes.label: rmk:yong->SWP

nodes.name: Stiff well-posedness is necessary and sufficient
nodes.statement: As indicated by \Cref{prop:not_SWP}, stiff well-posedness is a necessary stability criterion for \cref{eq} to have a correctly behaved asymptotic limit \cite{Yong_basic_2002}. \Cref{thm} shows that this necessary criterion is sufficient to imply the asymptotic convergence of slow variables.

nodes.name: Strong convergence despite oscillations
nodes.statement: As mentioned previously, dealing with high oscillations constitutes a challenging aspect of the problem. For multiscale problems with oscillatory or stochastic terms, one would typically expect convergence in the sense of weak convergence \cite{Fanelli2019Asymtptocs}, time averaging, or ensemble averaging \cite{Pavliotis2008Multiscale}. However, as demonstrated by the proof of \Cref{thm}, our findings reveal uniform convergence within a finite time $t$, thereby confirming the asymptotic convergence of slow variables over a finite time interval in the strong $L^\infty_t L^2_x$ sense under the unimprovable weakest stability condition. Notably, the solution to the reduced system \eqref{eq:reduced} is free of oscillations. Consequently, our results indicate that the oscillations in the slow variables, both in time and in space, are suppressed.
nodes.statement_short: Convergence is strong in $L^\infty_tL^2_x$, not weak or averaged; oscillations in slow variables are suppressed.

nodes.name: Implications for oscillatory multiscale systems
nodes.statement: The observed strong convergence inspires investigating systems characterized by high oscillation or fluctuation, as exemplified in molecular dynamics simulations. In contrast to the typically expected weak convergence, where physical quantities are accurate only in a statistical or average sense, strong convergence implies near-universal correctness pointwise. This insight enlightens the design and analysis of multiscale methods for oscillatory systems, providing a novel perspective and potential avenues for advancement.

nodes.name: Analogy with the Lax equivalence theorem
nodes.statement: Hyperbolic relaxation approximations \cite{JinXin1995relaxation,Natalini1996Convergence}, in our context, utilize hyperbolic relaxation systems \eqref{eq} to approximate reduced systems \eqref{eq:reduced} by introducing a small parameter $\varepsilon$. This idea parallels finite difference methods in numerical approximations, where convergence toward the solutions to \cref{eq:reduced} is considered as the mesh size approaches zero. In numerical analysis, the Lax equivalence theorem \cite{Lax1956Survey} is fundamental, stating that a consistent linear finite difference method for a well-posed linear initial value problem is convergent if it is stable. As highlighted in \Cref{prop:not_SWP}, stiff well-posedness is the most natural stability condition for hyperbolic relaxation approximations. From this perspective, \Cref{thm} establishes the Lax equivalence theorem for hyperbolic relaxation approximations.
nodes.statement_short: Relaxation approximations parallel finite differences; stiff well-posedness plays stability's role, so Theorem 3 is a Lax equivalence theorem.

nodes.name: Lax equivalence theorem
nodes.statement: In numerical analysis, the Lax equivalence theorem \cite{Lax1956Survey} is fundamental, stating that a consistent linear finite difference method for a well-posed linear initial value problem is convergent if it is stable.
assumptions: a consistent linear finite difference method for a well-posed linear initial value problem
conclusions: is convergent if it is stable.

nodes.statement: To obtain the error estimate in \Cref{thm}, we require uniform quasi-stability of the matrix set $\mathcal{F}_2$, which can be guaranteed by Yong's first stability condition without the non-oscillation assumption as discussed in \Cref{rmk:yong->SWP}.

nodes.name: Proof sketch of the main theorem (basic ideas)
nodes.statement: To enhance the clarity and comprehension of the proof of \Cref{thm}, let us begin by introducing some basic ideas within the proof. One crucial technique used in the proof is the Mori--Zwanzig technique \cite{E2011Principles,mori1965transport,zwanzig1960collision} to decouple fast and slow variables. This technique is a general strategy to integrate out a subset of variables in a problem. For \cref{eq}, this strategy can be employed as follows. Applying the Fourier transform on both sides of \eqref{eq} leads to the following system: \begin{displaymath} \od{\hat{U}}{t} = H \hat{U}, \quad \hat{U}(0, \xi, \eta) = \hat{U}_0(\xi), \end{displaymath} that is, \begin{gather*} \od{\hat{u}}{t} = H_{11} \hat{u} + H_{12} \hat{v}, \quad \hat{u}(0, \xi, \eta) = \hat{u}_0(\xi), \\ \od{\hat{v}}{t} = H_{21} \hat{u} + H_{22} \hat{v}, \quad \hat{v}(0, \xi, \eta) = \hat{v}_0(\xi). \end{gather*} Applying Duhamel's principle, one obtains that \begin{gather} \hat{u}(t, \xi, \eta) = \exp(H_{11} t) \hat{u}_0(\xi) + \int_0^t \exp(H_{11} (t - s)) H_{12} \hat{v}(s, \xi, \eta) \,\mathrm{d} s, \\ \hat{v}(t, \xi, \eta) = \exp(H_{22} t) \hat{v}_0(\xi) + \int_0^t \exp(H_{22} (t - s)) H_{21} \hat{u}(s, \xi, \eta) \,\mathrm{d} s, \end{gather} which yields that \begin{multline} \hat{u}(t, \xi, \eta) = \exp(H_{11} t) \hat{u}_0(\xi) \\ + G(t, \xi, \eta) \hat{v}_0(\xi) + \int_{0}^{t} G(t - s, \xi, \eta) H_{21} \hat{u}(s, \xi, \eta) \,\mathrm{d} s, \end{multline} where \begin{equation} G(t, \xi, \eta) := \int_{0}^{t} \exp ( H_{11} (t - s) ) H_{12} \exp(H_{22} s) \,\mathrm{d} s. \end{equation} Note that the first term on the right-hand side of \cref{eq:MZ} is the Fourier transform of the solution $\breve{u}$ to \cref{eq:reduced}. Therefore, we aim to demonstrate the $L^2$ norm of the sum of the second and third terms tends to zero as $\eta$ tends to infinity. The expressions of these terms highlight the importance of $G(t, \xi, \eta)$. At first glance, it suffices to establish that $G(t, \xi, \eta)$ vanishes in some sense in the asymptotic limit. Due to the stiff well-posedness of \cref{eq}, the matrix $B$ is quasi-stable. Recall that the matrix $H_{22}$ is defined as $H_{22} = H_{22}(\xi, \eta) = \eta B - i \sum_{j = 1}^n \xi_j A_{j, 22}$. The asymptotic behavior of $G(t, \xi, \eta)$ is somewhat analogous to the limit process in the Riemann--Lebesgue lemma. This observation involves replacing the scalar term that exhibits high-frequency oscillation in the canonical Riemann--Lebesgue lemma with a matrix exponential $\exp(H_{22}(\xi, \eta) t)$ that may exhibit high-frequency oscillation or rapid dissipation in the variable $t$ when $\eta$ is large. However, handling the matrix exponential in this form is challenging due to the non-commutative nature of the matrices $B$ and $A_{j, 22}$. By Laplace transform, we reduce this problem to resolvent estimates. Utilizing the improved resolvent estimates in \Cref{thm:IKMT} and estimates of an elementary integral in \Cref{lemma:integral}, we derive the generalized Riemann--Lebesgue lemma for matrix exponentials in \Cref{lemma:gRL}. According to this lemma, a uniform asymptotic convergence estimate of $G(t, \xi, \eta)$ is obtained in \Cref{lemma:low_frequency_G}, specifically at the low-frequency region, i.e., when the frequency $\xi$ is bounded. At this time, the low-frequency estimate of the error is summarized in \Cref{lemma:low_frequency}. When it comes to estimating the high-frequency error, the problem is more difficult. As mentioned in \Cref{rmk:yong->SWP}, if \cref{eq} satisfies Yong's first stability condition without the non-oscillation assumption, the two sets of matrices, $\mathcal{F}_1$ and $\mathcal{F}_2$, are uniformly quasi-stable, which yields at least that $G(t, \xi, \eta)$ is bounded by $|\xi|$ up to multiplication by a constant at the high-frequency region. At this time, the error at the high-frequency region can be controlled by taking a sufficiently large frequency truncation for the given initial value. However, when \cref{eq} only satisfies the condition of stiff well-posedness, one does not even know whether $G(t, \xi, \eta)$ is bounded, let alone control the high-frequency error. We solve this problem indirectly, by first establishing the uniform quasi-stability (UQS) of the matrix set $\mathcal{F}_1$, which is just the first conclusion of \Cref{thm}. We aim to prove that the matrix exponential $\exp(H_{11} t)$ is uniformly bounded. While \cref{eq:duhamel_u,eq:duhamel_v}, in accordance with stiff well-posedness, can be controlled uniformly for $t \ge 0$, $\xi \in \mathbb{R}^d$, and $\eta \ge 0$, these alone are insufficient to guarantee the uniform boundedness of the integral term of \cref{eq:duhamel_u}. It is important to note that the first right-hand term of \cref{eq:duhamel_u} is independent of $\eta$. The key in the proof is to examine the solution with zero initial value of fast variables and to show the integral term of \cref{eq:duhamel_u} tends to zero for fixed $t \ge 0$ and $\xi \in \mathbb{R}^d$ as $\eta$ tends to infinity. The asymptotic behavior of the integral term of \cref{eq:duhamel_v} is similar to our generalized Riemann--Lebesgue lemma in \Cref{lemma:gRL}. However, the integrand $\hat{u}$ depends on $\hat{v}$ according to \cref{eq:duhamel_u}, which brings additional challenges. Therefore, we utilize \cref{eq:duhamel_u,eq:duhamel_v} to construct a Picard sequence. By carefully choosing the Banach space and its subset being considered, we can prove that the iteration formula producing the Picard sequence is determined by a contraction mapping, which allows us to utilize the Banach fixed-point theorem to approximate the solution and to estimate it. In this way, one can obtain the uniform quasi-stability of the matrix set $\mathcal{F}_1$ as summarized in \Cref{lemma:UQS_of_F1}, which estimates the error at the high-frequency region in \Cref{lemma:high_frequency}. Together with \Cref{lemma:low_frequency}, one can complete the proof of \Cref{thm}.
nodes.statement_short: Mori-Zwanzig decoupling of slow and fast variables; low frequencies via a generalized Riemann-Lebesgue lemma, high frequencies via strong hyperbolicity of the reduced system from a Picard/Banach fixed-point argument.

nodes.statement: To enhance the clarity and comprehension of the proof of \Cref{thm}, let us begin by introducing some basic ideas within the proof.

nodes.name: Fourier transform
nodes.statement: One crucial technique used in the proof is the Mori--Zwanzig technique \cite{E2011Principles,mori1965transport,zwanzig1960collision} to decouple fast and slow variables. This technique is a general strategy to integrate out a subset of variables in a problem. For \cref{eq}, this strategy can be employed as follows. Applying the Fourier transform on both sides of \eqref{eq} leads to the following system: \begin{displaymath} \od{\hat{U}}{t} = H \hat{U}, \quad \hat{U}(0, \xi, \eta) = \hat{U}_0(\xi), \end{displaymath} that is, \begin{gather*} \od{\hat{u}}{t} = H_{11} \hat{u} + H_{12} \hat{v}, \quad \hat{u}(0, \xi, \eta) = \hat{u}_0(\xi), \\ \od{\hat{v}}{t} = H_{21} \hat{u} + H_{22} \hat{v}, \quad \hat{v}(0, \xi, \eta) = \hat{v}_0(\xi). \end{gather*}

nodes.name: Duhamel and key term
nodes.statement: Applying Duhamel's principle, one obtains that \begin{gather} \hat{u}(t, \xi, \eta) = \exp(H_{11} t) \hat{u}_0(\xi) + \int_0^t \exp(H_{11} (t - s)) H_{12} \hat{v}(s, \xi, \eta) \,\mathrm{d} s, \\ \hat{v}(t, \xi, \eta) = \exp(H_{22} t) \hat{v}_0(\xi) + \int_0^t \exp(H_{22} (t - s)) H_{21} \hat{u}(s, \xi, \eta) \,\mathrm{d} s, \end{gather} which yields that \begin{multline} \hat{u}(t, \xi, \eta) = \exp(H_{11} t) \hat{u}_0(\xi) \\ + G(t, \xi, \eta) \hat{v}_0(\xi) + \int_{0}^{t} G(t - s, \xi, \eta) H_{21} \hat{u}(s, \xi, \eta) \,\mathrm{d} s, \end{multline} where \begin{equation} G(t, \xi, \eta) := \int_{0}^{t} \exp ( H_{11} (t - s) ) H_{12} \exp(H_{22} s) \,\mathrm{d} s. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Apply Duhamel twice to get the Mori-Zwanzig equation and define $G$.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: Note that the first term on the right-hand side of \cref{eq:MZ} is the Fourier transform of the solution $\breve{u}$ to \cref{eq:reduced}. Therefore, we aim to demonstrate the $L^2$ norm of the sum of the second and third terms tends to zero as $\eta$ tends to infinity. The expressions of these terms highlight the importance of $G(t, \xi, \eta)$. At first glance, it suffices to establish that $G(t, \xi, \eta)$ vanishes in some sense in the asymptotic limit.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to showing $G$ vanishes asymptotically.

nodes.name: Riemann-Lebesgue analogy
nodes.statement: Due to the stiff well-posedness of \cref{eq}, the matrix $B$ is quasi-stable. Recall that the matrix $H_{22}$ is defined as $H_{22} = H_{22}(\xi, \eta) = \eta B - i \sum_{j = 1}^n \xi_j A_{j, 22}$. The asymptotic behavior of $G(t, \xi, \eta)$ is somewhat analogous to the limit process in the Riemann--Lebesgue lemma. This observation involves replacing the scalar term that exhibits high-frequency oscillation in the canonical Riemann--Lebesgue lemma with a matrix exponential $\exp(H_{22}(\xi, \eta) t)$ that may exhibit high-frequency oscillation or rapid dissipation in the variable $t$ when $\eta$ is large. However, handling the matrix exponential in this form is challenging due to the non-commutative nature of the matrices $B$ and $A_{j, 22}$.
nodes.statement_short: Analogy of $G$ with the Riemann-Lebesgue lemma; noncommutativity is the obstacle.

nodes.name: Low-frequency plan
nodes.statement: By Laplace transform, we reduce this problem to resolvent estimates. Utilizing the improved resolvent estimates in \Cref{thm:IKMT} and estimates of an elementary integral in \Cref{lemma:integral}, we derive the generalized Riemann--Lebesgue lemma for matrix exponentials in \Cref{lemma:gRL}. According to this lemma, a uniform asymptotic convergence estimate of $G(t, \xi, \eta)$ is obtained in \Cref{lemma:low_frequency_G}, specifically at the low-frequency region, i.e., when the frequency $\xi$ is bounded. At this time, the low-frequency estimate of the error is summarized in \Cref{lemma:low_frequency}.
nodes.statement_short: Laplace transform plus improved resolvent estimates give the low-frequency estimate.

nodes.name: High-frequency difficulty
nodes.statement: When it comes to estimating the high-frequency error, the problem is more difficult. As mentioned in \Cref{rmk:yong->SWP}, if \cref{eq} satisfies Yong's first stability condition without the non-oscillation assumption, the two sets of matrices, $\mathcal{F}_1$ and $\mathcal{F}_2$, are uniformly quasi-stable, which yields at least that $G(t, \xi, \eta)$ is bounded by $|\xi|$ up to multiplication by a constant at the high-frequency region. At this time, the error at the high-frequency region can be controlled by taking a sufficiently large frequency truncation for the given initial value. However, when \cref{eq} only satisfies the condition of stiff well-posedness, one does not even know whether $G(t, \xi, \eta)$ is bounded, let alone control the high-frequency error.
nodes.statement_short: Explain why high frequencies are hard under stiff well-posedness only.

nodes.name: Indirect approach
nodes.statement: We solve this problem indirectly, by first establishing the uniform quasi-stability (UQS) of the matrix set $\mathcal{F}_1$, which is just the first conclusion of \Cref{thm}. We aim to prove that the matrix exponential $\exp(H_{11} t)$ is uniformly bounded. While \cref{eq:duhamel_u,eq:duhamel_v}, in accordance with stiff well-posedness, can be controlled uniformly for $t \ge 0$, $\xi \in \mathbb{R}^d$, and $\eta \ge 0$, these alone are insufficient to guarantee the uniform boundedness of the integral term of \cref{eq:duhamel_u}. It is important to note that the first right-hand term of \cref{eq:duhamel_u} is independent of $\eta$. The key in the proof is to examine the solution with zero initial value of fast variables and to show the integral term of \cref{eq:duhamel_u} tends to zero for fixed $t \ge 0$ and $\xi \in \mathbb{R}^d$ as $\eta$ tends to infinity.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to uniform boundedness of $\exp(H_{11}t)$ with zero fast initial data.

nodes.name: Picard sequence and conclusion
nodes.statement: The asymptotic behavior of the integral term of \cref{eq:duhamel_v} is similar to our generalized Riemann--Lebesgue lemma in \Cref{lemma:gRL}. However, the integrand $\hat{u}$ depends on $\hat{v}$ according to \cref{eq:duhamel_u}, which brings additional challenges. Therefore, we utilize \cref{eq:duhamel_u,eq:duhamel_v} to construct a Picard sequence. By carefully choosing the Banach space and its subset being considered, we can prove that the iteration formula producing the Picard sequence is determined by a contraction mapping, which allows us to utilize the Banach fixed-point theorem to approximate the solution and to estimate it. In this way, one can obtain the uniform quasi-stability of the matrix set $\mathcal{F}_1$ as summarized in \Cref{lemma:UQS_of_F1}, which estimates the error at the high-frequency region in \Cref{lemma:high_frequency}. Together with \Cref{lemma:low_frequency}, one can complete the proof of \Cref{thm}.
nodes.statement_short: Picard iteration and Banach fixed point give UQS of $\mathcal{F}_1$; combine high and low frequency.

nodes.name: Elementary integral I
nodes.statement: Let us begin with basic estimates of the following integral: \begin{equation} \mathcal{I}(\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \beta_1, \beta_2) := \int_{- \infty}^{+ \infty} \frac{1}{|y - \alpha_1| + \beta_1} \cdot \frac{1}{|y - \alpha_2| + \beta_2} \,\mathrm{d} y. \end{equation} Here, $\alpha_j \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\beta_j > 0$ for $j = 1, 2$.

nodes.name: Generalized Riemann-Lebesgue lemma for matrix exponentials
nodes.statement: Assume that the $r \times r$ matrix $B$ is invertible and quasi-stable, the $r \times r$ matrix $M$ is arbitrary, and the function $f \in C^1([0, T])$ for a fixed $T > 0$. The following estimate holds for $\eta \ge 6 \gamma \delta^{-1}$: \begin{displaymath} \bigg\| \int_0^T \exp \big( (\eta B + M) (T - s) \big) f(s) \,\mathrm{d} s \bigg\| \le \frac{32 \sqrt{2} r K e^{\gamma T}} {\pi \eta \delta} \|f\|_{C^1([0, T])} \log \frac{\eta \delta + \gamma}{\gamma}, \end{displaymath} where $K$ and $\delta$ depend on the matrix $B$, and $\gamma = 2 K \norm{M} + 1$. Furthermore, if the matrix $M$ and the function $f \in C^1([0, +\infty))$ take the form of \begin{displaymath} M = M(\theta) = \sum_{j = 1}^d \theta_j M_j, \quad f = f(\cdot; \theta), \end{displaymath} respectively, where $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^d$, the matrices $M_j$ with $j = 1, 2, \ldots, d$ are chosen such that the set of matrices, \begin{displaymath} \mathcal{F} = \left\{ \eta B + M(\theta) \,\big|\, \theta \in \mathbb{R}^d, \eta \ge 0 \right\}, \end{displaymath} is uniformly quasi-stable, and the function $f(\cdot; \theta)$ satisfies \begin{displaymath} f(\cdot; \omega \theta) = f(\omega \cdot; \theta), \end{displaymath} for each $\omega > 0$, then the following estimate holds for $\eta >\beta (|\theta| + 1)$: \begin{multline*} \bigg\| \int_0^T \exp \big( (\eta B + M(\theta)) (T - s) \big) f(s; \theta) \,\mathrm{d} s \bigg\| \\ \le \frac{16 \sqrt{2} r \tilde{K} e^T}{\pi \eta \tilde{\delta}} \sup_{|\theta| = 1} \|f(\cdot; \theta)\|_{C^1([0, T])} \log(\eta \tilde{\delta} + 1), \end{multline*} where $\tilde{K} > 0$ and $\beta > 0$ depend on the matrix set $\mathcal{F}$, and $\tilde{\delta} > 0$ depends on the matrix $B$.

nodes.name: Proof of the generalized Riemann-Lebesgue lemma
nodes.statement: For a complex number $z \in \mathbb{C}$, let us denote its real part and imaginary part by $\gamma = \Re(z)$ and $y = \Im(z)$, respectively, i.e., $z = \gamma + i y$ with $\gamma, y \in \mathbb{R}$. We consider the zero extension of the function $f$, i.e., we define the value of $f(t)$ as $f(t) \equiv 0$ for each $t > T$, and we still use the notation $f(t)$. The Laplace transform $\tilde{f}(z)$ of $f(t)$ is given as follows, \begin{multline*} \tilde{f}(z) := \int_0^T e^{- z t} f(t) \,\mathrm{d} t = \int_0^T e^{- i t y} e^{- \gamma t} f(t) \,\mathrm{d} t \\ = \left( \frac{1}{- i y} e^{-i t y} e^{- \gamma t} f(t) \right) \bigg|_{t = 0}^{t = T} - \int_0^T \frac{1}{- i y} e^{- i t y} \od{}{t} \left( e^{- \gamma t} f(t) \right) \,\mathrm{d} t, \end{multline*} which yields the following estimate of $\tilde{f}(z)$: \begin{multline*} |\tilde{f}(z)| \le \min \left\{ \frac{1}{\gamma}, \frac{2 + \gamma^{-1} + e^{- \gamma T}}{|y|} \right\} \|f\|_{C^1([0,T])} \\ \le \min \left\{ \frac{1}{\gamma}, \frac{4}{|y|} \right\} \|f\|_{C^1([0,T])} \le \frac{8 \|f\|_{C^1([0,T])}}{|y| + 4 \gamma}, \end{multline*} where the constant $\gamma > 1$ is to be determined. The Laplace transform $\tilde{R}(z)$ of the function $R(t)$ defined as \begin{displaymath} R(t) = \int_0^t \exp \big( (\eta B + M)(t - s) \big) f(s) \,\mathrm{d} s, \end{displaymath} is given by \begin{displaymath} \tilde{R}(z) = \int_0^{+\infty} e^{- z t} R(t) \,\mathrm{d} t = (z I - \eta B - M)^{-1} \tilde{f}(z). \end{displaymath} By the inverse Laplace transform, one can obtain that \begin{multline*} R(t) = \frac{1}{2 \pi i} \int_{\gamma - i \infty}^{\gamma + i \infty} e^{t z} \tilde{R}(z) \,\mathrm{d} z = \frac{e^{\gamma t}}{2 \pi} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} e^{i t y} (z I - \eta B - M)^{-1} \tilde{f}(z) \,\mathrm{d} y \\ = \frac{e^{\gamma t}}{2 \pi} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} e^{i t y} \big( I - (z I - \eta B)^{-1} M \big)^{-1} (z I - \eta B)^{-1} \tilde{f}(z) \,\mathrm{d} y. \end{multline*} Since the matrix $B$ is quasi-stable, the set of matrices $\eta B$ with $\eta \ge 0$ is uniformly quasi-stable. By \Cref{thm:IKMT}, there exists a constant $K > 0$ such that \begin{displaymath} \|(z I - \eta B)^{-1}\| \le K \max_{\lambda \in \sigma(B)} |z - \eta \lambda|^{-1} \le \frac{K}{\gamma}. \end{displaymath} By taking $\gamma = 2 K \|M\| + 1$, one can obtain that \begin{displaymath} \|(z I - \eta B)^{-1} M\| \le \frac{K \|M\|}{\gamma} < \frac12, \end{displaymath} and thus, \begin{displaymath} \big\| \big( I - (z I - \eta B)^{-1} M \big)^{-1} \big\| < 2. \end{displaymath} Therefore, \begin{multline*} \|R(T)\| \le \frac{e^{\gamma T}}{2 \pi} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \big\| \big( I - (z I - \eta B)^{-1} M \big)^{-1} \big\| \cdot \|(z I - \eta B)^{-1}\| \cdot |\tilde{f}(z)| \,\mathrm{d} y \\ \le \frac{K e^{\gamma T}}{\pi} \|f\|_{C^1([0, T])} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \max_{\lambda \in \sigma(B)} |z - \eta \lambda|^{-1} \frac{8}{|y| + 4 \gamma} \,\mathrm{d} y \\ \le \frac{8 \sqrt{2} K e^{\gamma T}}{\pi} \|f\|_{C^1([0, T])} \sum_{\lambda \in \sigma(B)} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \frac{1}{|y - \eta \Im(\lambda)| + \gamma - \eta \Re(\lambda)} \cdot \frac{1}{|y| + 4 \gamma} \,\mathrm{d} y \\ = \frac{8 \sqrt{2} K e^{\gamma T}}{\pi} \|f\|_{C^1([0, T])} \sum_{\lambda \in \sigma(B)} \mathcal{I}(\eta \Im(\lambda), 0, \gamma - \eta \Re(\lambda), 4 \gamma). \end{multline*} Note that the matrix $B$ is invertible and quasi-stable, there exists a constant $\delta > 0$ dependent on $B$ such that for each eigenvalue $\lambda \in \sigma(B)$ either $\Re(\lambda) \le - \delta$ or $|\Im(\lambda)| \ge \delta$ holds. If $\Re(\lambda) \le - \delta$, then \begin{displaymath} \mathcal{I}(\eta \Im(\lambda), 0, \gamma - \eta \Re(\lambda), 4 \gamma) \le \mathcal{I}(\eta \Im(\lambda), 0, \gamma + \eta \delta, 4 \gamma) \le \frac{2}{\eta \delta - 3 \gamma} \log \frac{\eta \delta + \gamma}{4 \gamma}. \end{displaymath} If $|\Im(\lambda)| \ge \delta$, then \begin{displaymath} \mathcal{I}(\eta \Im(\lambda), 0, \gamma - \eta \Re(\lambda), 4 \gamma) \le \mathcal{I}(\eta \delta, 0, \gamma, \gamma) \le \frac{4 (\eta \delta + \gamma)} {\eta \delta (\eta \delta + 2 \gamma)} \log \frac{\eta \delta + \gamma}{\gamma}. \end{displaymath} Both cases yield that \begin{displaymath} \mathcal{I}(\eta \Im(\lambda), 0, \gamma - \eta \Re(\lambda), 4 \gamma) \le \frac{4}{\eta \delta} \log \frac{\eta \delta + \gamma}{\gamma}, \end{displaymath} as long as $\eta \delta \ge 6 \gamma$, which completes the proof of the first conclusion of this lemma. Let us now prove the second conclusion of this lemma. The Laplace transform of $f(t; \theta)$ satisfies the following scaling property: \begin{displaymath} \tilde{f}(z; \omega \theta) = \omega^{-1} \tilde{f}(\omega^{-1} z; \theta), \end{displaymath} for each $\omega > 0$, which yields the following estimate: \begin{displaymath} |\tilde{f}(z; \theta)| \le \frac{8}{|y| + 4 \gamma} \|f(\cdot; |\theta|^{-1} \theta)\|_{C^1([0, +\infty))}. \end{displaymath} By applying \Cref{thm:IKMT} on the uniformly quasi-stable matrix set $\mathcal{F}$ and using the previous arguments, one can obtain the following estimate: \begin{multline*} \|R(T; \theta)\| \le \frac{4 \sqrt{2} \tilde{K} e^{\tilde{\gamma} T}}{\pi} \sup_{|\theta| = 1} \|f(\cdot; \theta)\|_{C^1([0, +\infty))} \\ \sum_{\lambda \in \sigma(\eta B + M(\theta))} \mathcal{I}(\Im(\lambda), 0, \tilde{\gamma} - \Re(\lambda), 4 \tilde{\gamma}), \end{multline*} where $\tilde{\gamma} > 0$ is arbitrary and to be determined, and $\tilde{K} > 0$ depends on the matrix set $\mathcal{F}$. Since the matrix $B$ is invertible, there exist constants $\tilde{\alpha} > 0$ and $\tilde{\delta} > 0$ dependent on the matrix set $\mathcal{F}$ such that if $|\theta| \le \tilde{\alpha} \eta$, then for each eigenvalue $\lambda \in \sigma(\eta B + M(\theta))$ either $\Re(\lambda) \le - \eta \tilde{\delta}$ or $|\Im(\lambda)| \ge \eta \tilde{\delta}$ holds. If $\Re(\lambda) \le - \eta \tilde{\delta}$, then \begin{displaymath} \mathcal{I}(\Im(\lambda), 0, \tilde{\gamma} - \Re(\lambda), 4 \tilde{\gamma}) \le \mathcal{I}(\Im(\lambda), 0, \tilde{\gamma} + \eta \tilde{\delta}, 4 \tilde{\gamma}) \le \frac{2}{\eta \tilde{\delta} - 3 \tilde{\gamma}} \log \frac{\eta \tilde{\delta} + \tilde{\gamma}}{4 \tilde{\gamma}}. \end{displaymath} If $|\Im(\lambda)| \ge \eta \tilde{\delta}$, then \begin{displaymath} \mathcal{I}(\Im(\lambda), 0, \tilde{\gamma} - \Re(\lambda), 4 \tilde{\gamma}) \le \mathcal{I}(\eta \tilde{\delta}, 0, \tilde{\gamma}, \tilde{\gamma}) \le \frac{4 (\eta \tilde{\delta} + \tilde{\gamma})} {\eta \tilde{\delta} (\eta \tilde{\delta} + 2 \tilde{\gamma})} \log \frac{\eta \tilde{\delta} + \tilde{\gamma}}{\tilde{\gamma}}. \end{displaymath} Both cases yield that \begin{displaymath} \mathcal{I}(\Im(\lambda), 0, \tilde{\gamma} - \Re(\lambda), \tilde{\alpha}_2) \le \frac{4}{\eta \tilde{\delta}} \log \frac{\eta \tilde{\delta} + \tilde{\gamma}}{\tilde{\gamma}}, \end{displaymath} as long as $\eta \tilde{\delta} \ge 6 \tilde{\gamma}$. One can choose $\tilde{\gamma} = 1$, and then obtain the desired result.
nodes.statement_short: Laplace transform turns the integral into a resolvent contour integral; improved Kreiss resolvent bounds and the elementary integral estimates give decay. Key step: splitting eigenvalues of $B$ into dissipative ($\Re\lambda\le-\delta$) and oscillatory ($|\Im\lambda|\ge\delta$).

The Laplace transform $\tilde{f}(z)$ of $f(t)$ is given as follows, \begin{multline*} \tilde{f}(z) := \int_0^T e^{- z t} f(t) \,\mathrm{d} t = \int_0^T e^{- i t y} e^{- \gamma t} f(t) \,\mathrm{d} t \\ = \left( \frac{1}{- i y} e^{-i t y} e^{- \gamma t} f(t) \right) \bigg|_{t = 0}^{t = T} - \int_0^T \frac{1}{- i y} e^{- i t y} \od{}{t} \left( e^{- \gamma t} f(t) \right) \,\mathrm{d} t, \end{multline*} which yields the following estimate of $\tilde{f}(z)$: \begin{multline*} |\tilde{f}(z)| \le \min \left\{ \frac{1}{\gamma}, \frac{2 + \gamma^{-1} + e^{- \gamma T}}{|y|} \right\} \|f\|_{C^1([0,T])} \\ \le \min \left\{ \frac{1}{\gamma}, \frac{4}{|y|} \right\} \|f\|_{C^1([0,T])} \le \frac{8 \|f\|_{C^1([0,T])}}{|y| + 4 \gamma}, \end{multline*} where the constant $\gamma > 1$ is to be determined. The Laplace transform $\tilde{R}(z)$ of the function $R(t)$ defined as \begin{displaymath} R(t) = \int_0^t \exp \big( (\eta B + M)(t - s) \big) f(s) \,\mathrm{d} s, \end{displaymath} is given by \begin{displaymath} \tilde{R}(z) = \int_0^{+\infty} e^{- z t} R(t) \,\mathrm{d} t = (z I - \eta B - M)^{-1} \tilde{f}(z). \end{displaymath} By the inverse Laplace transform, one can obtain that \begin{multline*} R(t) = \frac{1}{2 \pi i} \int_{\gamma - i \infty}^{\gamma + i \infty} e^{t z} \tilde{R}(z) \,\mathrm{d} z = \frac{e^{\gamma t}}{2 \pi} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} e^{i t y} (z I - \eta B - M)^{-1} \tilde{f}(z) \,\mathrm{d} y \\ = \frac{e^{\gamma t}}{2 \pi} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} e^{i t y} \big( I - (z I - \eta B)^{-1} M \big)^{-1} (z I - \eta B)^{-1} \tilde{f}(z) \,\mathrm{d} y. \end{multline*} Since the matrix $B$ is quasi-stable, the set of matrices $\eta B$ with $\eta \ge 0$ is uniformly quasi-stable. By \Cref{thm:IKMT}, there exists a constant $K > 0$ such that \begin{displaymath} \|(z I - \eta B)^{-1}\| \le K \max_{\lambda \in \sigma(B)} |z - \eta \lambda|^{-1} \le \frac{K}{\gamma}. \end{displaymath} By taking $\gamma = 2 K \|M\| + 1$, one can obtain that \begin{displaymath} \|(z I - \eta B)^{-1} M\| \le \frac{K \|M\|}{\gamma} < \frac12, \end{displaymath} and thus, \begin{displaymath} \big\| \big( I - (z I - \eta B)^{-1} M \big)^{-1} \big\| < 2. \end{displaymath} Therefore, \begin{multline*} \|R(T)\| \le \frac{e^{\gamma T}}{2 \pi} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \big\| \big( I - (z I - \eta B)^{-1} M \big)^{-1} \big\| \cdot \|(z I - \eta B)^{-1}\| \cdot |\tilde{f}(z)| \,\mathrm{d} y \\ \le \frac{K e^{\gamma T}}{\pi} \|f\|_{C^1([0, T])} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \max_{\lambda \in \sigma(B)} |z - \eta \lambda|^{-1} \frac{8}{|y| + 4 \gamma} \,\mathrm{d} y \\ \le \frac{8 \sqrt{2} K e^{\gamma T}}{\pi} \|f\|_{C^1([0, T])} \sum_{\lambda \in \sigma(B)} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \frac{1}{|y - \eta \Im(\lambda)| + \gamma - \eta \Re(\lambda)} \cdot \frac{1}{|y| + 4 \gamma} \,\mathrm{d} y \\ = \frac{8 \sqrt{2} K e^{\gamma T}}{\pi} \|f\|_{C^1([0, T])} \sum_{\lambda \in \sigma(B)} \mathcal{I}(\eta \Im(\lambda), 0, \gamma - \eta \Re(\lambda), 4 \gamma). \end{multline*} Note that the matrix $B$ is invertible and quasi-stable, there exists a constant $\delta > 0$ dependent on $B$ such that for each eigenvalue $\lambda \in \sigma(B)$ either $\Re(\lambda) \le - \delta$ or $|\Im(\lambda)| \ge \delta$ holds. If $\Re(\lambda) \le - \delta$, then \begin{displaymath} \mathcal{I}(\eta \Im(\lambda), 0, \gamma - \eta \Re(\lambda), 4 \gamma) \le \mathcal{I}(\eta \Im(\lambda), 0, \gamma + \eta \delta, 4 \gamma) \le \frac{2}{\eta \delta - 3 \gamma} \log \frac{\eta \delta + \gamma}{4 \gamma}. \end{displaymath} If $|\Im(\lambda)| \ge \delta$, then \begin{displaymath} \mathcal{I}(\eta \Im(\lambda), 0, \gamma - \eta \Re(\lambda), 4 \gamma) \le \mathcal{I}(\eta \delta, 0, \gamma, \gamma) \le \frac{4 (\eta \delta + \gamma)} {\eta \delta (\eta \delta + 2 \gamma)} \log \frac{\eta \delta + \gamma}{\gamma}. \end{displaymath} Both cases yield that \begin{displaymath} \mathcal{I}(\eta \Im(\lambda), 0, \gamma - \eta \Re(\lambda), 4 \gamma) \le \frac{4}{\eta \delta} \log \frac{\eta \delta + \gamma}{\gamma}, \end{displaymath} as long as $\eta \delta \ge 6 \gamma$, which completes the proof of the first conclusion of this lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Prove the fixed-$M$ estimate.

nodes.name: Notation and zero extension
nodes.statement: For a complex number $z \in \mathbb{C}$, let us denote its real part and imaginary part by $\gamma = \Re(z)$ and $y = \Im(z)$, respectively, i.e., $z = \gamma + i y$ with $\gamma, y \in \mathbb{R}$. We consider the zero extension of the function $f$, i.e., we define the value of $f(t)$ as $f(t) \equiv 0$ for each $t > T$, and we still use the notation $f(t)$.
nodes.statement_short: Write $z=\gamma+iy$ and extend $f$ by zero.

nodes.name: Laplace transform bound
nodes.statement: The Laplace transform $\tilde{f}(z)$ of $f(t)$ is given as follows, \begin{multline*} \tilde{f}(z) := \int_0^T e^{- z t} f(t) \,\mathrm{d} t = \int_0^T e^{- i t y} e^{- \gamma t} f(t) \,\mathrm{d} t \\ = \left( \frac{1}{- i y} e^{-i t y} e^{- \gamma t} f(t) \right) \bigg|_{t = 0}^{t = T} - \int_0^T \frac{1}{- i y} e^{- i t y} \od{}{t} \left( e^{- \gamma t} f(t) \right) \,\mathrm{d} t, \end{multline*} which yields the following estimate of $\tilde{f}(z)$: \begin{multline*} |\tilde{f}(z)| \le \min \left\{ \frac{1}{\gamma}, \frac{2 + \gamma^{-1} + e^{- \gamma T}}{|y|} \right\} \|f\|_{C^1([0,T])} \\ \le \min \left\{ \frac{1}{\gamma}, \frac{4}{|y|} \right\} \|f\|_{C^1([0,T])} \le \frac{8 \|f\|_{C^1([0,T])}}{|y| + 4 \gamma}, \end{multline*} where the constant $\gamma > 1$ is to be determined.
nodes.statement_short: Integrate by parts to bound $|\tilde f(z)|\le 8\|f\|_{C^1}/(|y|+4\gamma)$.

nodes.name: Laplace transform of R
nodes.statement: The Laplace transform $\tilde{R}(z)$ of the function $R(t)$ defined as \begin{displaymath} R(t) = \int_0^t \exp \big( (\eta B + M)(t - s) \big) f(s) \,\mathrm{d} s, \end{displaymath} is given by \begin{displaymath} \tilde{R}(z) = \int_0^{+\infty} e^{- z t} R(t) \,\mathrm{d} t = (z I - \eta B - M)^{-1} \tilde{f}(z). \end{displaymath}
nodes.statement_short: Express $\tilde R$ through the resolvent.

nodes.name: Inverse Laplace transform
nodes.statement: By the inverse Laplace transform, one can obtain that \begin{multline*} R(t) = \frac{1}{2 \pi i} \int_{\gamma - i \infty}^{\gamma + i \infty} e^{t z} \tilde{R}(z) \,\mathrm{d} z = \frac{e^{\gamma t}}{2 \pi} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} e^{i t y} (z I - \eta B - M)^{-1} \tilde{f}(z) \,\mathrm{d} y \\ = \frac{e^{\gamma t}}{2 \pi} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} e^{i t y} \big( I - (z I - \eta B)^{-1} M \big)^{-1} (z I - \eta B)^{-1} \tilde{f}(z) \,\mathrm{d} y. \end{multline*}
nodes.statement_short: Invert and factor the resolvent of $\eta B+M$.

nodes.name: Apply improved resolvent estimate
nodes.statement: Since the matrix $B$ is quasi-stable, the set of matrices $\eta B$ with $\eta \ge 0$ is uniformly quasi-stable. By \Cref{thm:IKMT}, there exists a constant $K > 0$ such that \begin{displaymath} \|(z I - \eta B)^{-1}\| \le K \max_{\lambda \in \sigma(B)} |z - \eta \lambda|^{-1} \le \frac{K}{\gamma}. \end{displaymath}
nodes.statement_short: Apply Theorem 2 to $\{\eta B\}$.

nodes.name: Neumann series bound
nodes.statement: By taking $\gamma = 2 K \|M\| + 1$, one can obtain that \begin{displaymath} \|(z I - \eta B)^{-1} M\| \le \frac{K \|M\|}{\gamma} < \frac12, \end{displaymath} and thus, \begin{displaymath} \big\| \big( I - (z I - \eta B)^{-1} M \big)^{-1} \big\| < 2. \end{displaymath}
nodes.statement_short: Choose $\gamma$ so the perturbation factor is bounded by 2.

nodes.name: Reduce to elementary integrals
nodes.statement: Therefore, \begin{multline*} \|R(T)\| \le \frac{e^{\gamma T}}{2 \pi} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \big\| \big( I - (z I - \eta B)^{-1} M \big)^{-1} \big\| \cdot \|(z I - \eta B)^{-1}\| \cdot |\tilde{f}(z)| \,\mathrm{d} y \\ \le \frac{K e^{\gamma T}}{\pi} \|f\|_{C^1([0, T])} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \max_{\lambda \in \sigma(B)} |z - \eta \lambda|^{-1} \frac{8}{|y| + 4 \gamma} \,\mathrm{d} y \\ \le \frac{8 \sqrt{2} K e^{\gamma T}}{\pi} \|f\|_{C^1([0, T])} \sum_{\lambda \in \sigma(B)} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \frac{1}{|y - \eta \Im(\lambda)| + \gamma - \eta \Re(\lambda)} \cdot \frac{1}{|y| + 4 \gamma} \,\mathrm{d} y \\ = \frac{8 \sqrt{2} K e^{\gamma T}}{\pi} \|f\|_{C^1([0, T])} \sum_{\lambda \in \sigma(B)} \mathcal{I}(\eta \Im(\lambda), 0, \gamma - \eta \Re(\lambda), 4 \gamma). \end{multline*}
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\|R(T)\|$ by a sum of integrals $\mathcal{I}$.

nodes.name: Spectral gap delta
nodes.statement: Note that the matrix $B$ is invertible and quasi-stable, there exists a constant $\delta > 0$ dependent on $B$ such that for each eigenvalue $\lambda \in \sigma(B)$ either $\Re(\lambda) \le - \delta$ or $|\Im(\lambda)| \ge \delta$ holds.
nodes.statement_short: Every eigenvalue is dissipative or oscillatory with margin $\delta$.

nodes.name: Dissipative case
nodes.statement: If $\Re(\lambda) \le - \delta$, then \begin{displaymath} \mathcal{I}(\eta \Im(\lambda), 0, \gamma - \eta \Re(\lambda), 4 \gamma) \le \mathcal{I}(\eta \Im(\lambda), 0, \gamma + \eta \delta, 4 \gamma) \le \frac{2}{\eta \delta - 3 \gamma} \log \frac{\eta \delta + \gamma}{4 \gamma}. \end{displaymath}
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\mathcal{I}$ for dissipative eigenvalues.

nodes.name: Oscillatory case
nodes.statement: If $|\Im(\lambda)| \ge \delta$, then \begin{displaymath} \mathcal{I}(\eta \Im(\lambda), 0, \gamma - \eta \Re(\lambda), 4 \gamma) \le \mathcal{I}(\eta \delta, 0, \gamma, \gamma) \le \frac{4 (\eta \delta + \gamma)} {\eta \delta (\eta \delta + 2 \gamma)} \log \frac{\eta \delta + \gamma}{\gamma}. \end{displaymath}
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\mathcal{I}$ for oscillatory eigenvalues.

nodes.name: Conclude first part
nodes.statement: Both cases yield that \begin{displaymath} \mathcal{I}(\eta \Im(\lambda), 0, \gamma - \eta \Re(\lambda), 4 \gamma) \le \frac{4}{\eta \delta} \log \frac{\eta \delta + \gamma}{\gamma}, \end{displaymath} as long as $\eta \delta \ge 6 \gamma$, which completes the proof of the first conclusion of this lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Both cases give $4(\eta\delta)^{-1}\log(\cdot)$ for $\eta\delta\ge6\gamma$.

nodes.name: Second conclusion
nodes.statement: Let us now prove the second conclusion of this lemma. The Laplace transform of $f(t; \theta)$ satisfies the following scaling property: \begin{displaymath} \tilde{f}(z; \omega \theta) = \omega^{-1} \tilde{f}(\omega^{-1} z; \theta), \end{displaymath} for each $\omega > 0$, which yields the following estimate: \begin{displaymath} |\tilde{f}(z; \theta)| \le \frac{8}{|y| + 4 \gamma} \|f(\cdot; |\theta|^{-1} \theta)\|_{C^1([0, +\infty))}. \end{displaymath} By applying \Cref{thm:IKMT} on the uniformly quasi-stable matrix set $\mathcal{F}$ and using the previous arguments, one can obtain the following estimate: \begin{multline*} \|R(T; \theta)\| \le \frac{4 \sqrt{2} \tilde{K} e^{\tilde{\gamma} T}}{\pi} \sup_{|\theta| = 1} \|f(\cdot; \theta)\|_{C^1([0, +\infty))} \\ \sum_{\lambda \in \sigma(\eta B + M(\theta))} \mathcal{I}(\Im(\lambda), 0, \tilde{\gamma} - \Re(\lambda), 4 \tilde{\gamma}), \end{multline*} where $\tilde{\gamma} > 0$ is arbitrary and to be determined, and $\tilde{K} > 0$ depends on the matrix set $\mathcal{F}$. Since the matrix $B$ is invertible, there exist constants $\tilde{\alpha} > 0$ and $\tilde{\delta} > 0$ dependent on the matrix set $\mathcal{F}$ such that if $|\theta| \le \tilde{\alpha} \eta$, then for each eigenvalue $\lambda \in \sigma(\eta B + M(\theta))$ either $\Re(\lambda) \le - \eta \tilde{\delta}$ or $|\Im(\lambda)| \ge \eta \tilde{\delta}$ holds. If $\Re(\lambda) \le - \eta \tilde{\delta}$, then \begin{displaymath} \mathcal{I}(\Im(\lambda), 0, \tilde{\gamma} - \Re(\lambda), 4 \tilde{\gamma}) \le \mathcal{I}(\Im(\lambda), 0, \tilde{\gamma} + \eta \tilde{\delta}, 4 \tilde{\gamma}) \le \frac{2}{\eta \tilde{\delta} - 3 \tilde{\gamma}} \log \frac{\eta \tilde{\delta} + \tilde{\gamma}}{4 \tilde{\gamma}}. \end{displaymath} If $|\Im(\lambda)| \ge \eta \tilde{\delta}$, then \begin{displaymath} \mathcal{I}(\Im(\lambda), 0, \tilde{\gamma} - \Re(\lambda), 4 \tilde{\gamma}) \le \mathcal{I}(\eta \tilde{\delta}, 0, \tilde{\gamma}, \tilde{\gamma}) \le \frac{4 (\eta \tilde{\delta} + \tilde{\gamma})} {\eta \tilde{\delta} (\eta \tilde{\delta} + 2 \tilde{\gamma})} \log \frac{\eta \tilde{\delta} + \tilde{\gamma}}{\tilde{\gamma}}. \end{displaymath} Both cases yield that \begin{displaymath} \mathcal{I}(\Im(\lambda), 0, \tilde{\gamma} - \Re(\lambda), \tilde{\alpha}_2) \le \frac{4}{\eta \tilde{\delta}} \log \frac{\eta \tilde{\delta} + \tilde{\gamma}}{\tilde{\gamma}}, \end{displaymath} as long as $\eta \tilde{\delta} \ge 6 \tilde{\gamma}$. One can choose $\tilde{\gamma} = 1$, and then obtain the desired result.
nodes.statement_short: Prove the uniform-in-$\theta$ estimate.

nodes.name: Scaling of Laplace transform
nodes.statement: The Laplace transform of $f(t; \theta)$ satisfies the following scaling property: \begin{displaymath} \tilde{f}(z; \omega \theta) = \omega^{-1} \tilde{f}(\omega^{-1} z; \theta), \end{displaymath} for each $\omega > 0$, which yields the following estimate: \begin{displaymath} |\tilde{f}(z; \theta)| \le \frac{8}{|y| + 4 \gamma} \|f(\cdot; |\theta|^{-1} \theta)\|_{C^1([0, +\infty))}. \end{displaymath}
nodes.statement_short: Use homogeneity of $f$ to bound $\tilde f(z;\theta)$.

nodes.name: Apply improved resolvent estimate uniformly
nodes.statement: By applying \Cref{thm:IKMT} on the uniformly quasi-stable matrix set $\mathcal{F}$ and using the previous arguments, one can obtain the following estimate: \begin{multline*} \|R(T; \theta)\| \le \frac{4 \sqrt{2} \tilde{K} e^{\tilde{\gamma} T}}{\pi} \sup_{|\theta| = 1} \|f(\cdot; \theta)\|_{C^1([0, +\infty))} \\ \sum_{\lambda \in \sigma(\eta B + M(\theta))} \mathcal{I}(\Im(\lambda), 0, \tilde{\gamma} - \Re(\lambda), 4 \tilde{\gamma}), \end{multline*} where $\tilde{\gamma} > 0$ is arbitrary and to be determined, and $\tilde{K} > 0$ depends on the matrix set $\mathcal{F}$.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 2 on $\mathcal{F}$ reduces to elementary integrals.

nodes.name: Uniform spectral gap
nodes.statement: Since the matrix $B$ is invertible, there exist constants $\tilde{\alpha} > 0$ and $\tilde{\delta} > 0$ dependent on the matrix set $\mathcal{F}$ such that if $|\theta| \le \tilde{\alpha} \eta$, then for each eigenvalue $\lambda \in \sigma(\eta B + M(\theta))$ either $\Re(\lambda) \le - \eta \tilde{\delta}$ or $|\Im(\lambda)| \ge \eta \tilde{\delta}$ holds.
nodes.statement_short: For $|\theta|\le\tilde\alpha\eta$ eigenvalues are dissipative or oscillatory with margin $\eta\tilde\delta$.

nodes.name: Dissipative case
nodes.statement: If $\Re(\lambda) \le - \eta \tilde{\delta}$, then \begin{displaymath} \mathcal{I}(\Im(\lambda), 0, \tilde{\gamma} - \Re(\lambda), 4 \tilde{\gamma}) \le \mathcal{I}(\Im(\lambda), 0, \tilde{\gamma} + \eta \tilde{\delta}, 4 \tilde{\gamma}) \le \frac{2}{\eta \tilde{\delta} - 3 \tilde{\gamma}} \log \frac{\eta \tilde{\delta} + \tilde{\gamma}}{4 \tilde{\gamma}}. \end{displaymath}
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\mathcal{I}$ for dissipative eigenvalues.

nodes.name: Oscillatory case
nodes.statement: If $|\Im(\lambda)| \ge \eta \tilde{\delta}$, then \begin{displaymath} \mathcal{I}(\Im(\lambda), 0, \tilde{\gamma} - \Re(\lambda), 4 \tilde{\gamma}) \le \mathcal{I}(\eta \tilde{\delta}, 0, \tilde{\gamma}, \tilde{\gamma}) \le \frac{4 (\eta \tilde{\delta} + \tilde{\gamma})} {\eta \tilde{\delta} (\eta \tilde{\delta} + 2 \tilde{\gamma})} \log \frac{\eta \tilde{\delta} + \tilde{\gamma}}{\tilde{\gamma}}. \end{displaymath}
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\mathcal{I}$ for oscillatory eigenvalues.

nodes.name: Conclude second part
nodes.statement: Both cases yield that \begin{displaymath} \mathcal{I}(\Im(\lambda), 0, \tilde{\gamma} - \Re(\lambda), \tilde{\alpha}_2) \le \frac{4}{\eta \tilde{\delta}} \log \frac{\eta \tilde{\delta} + \tilde{\gamma}}{\tilde{\gamma}}, \end{displaymath} as long as $\eta \tilde{\delta} \ge 6 \tilde{\gamma}$. One can choose $\tilde{\gamma} = 1$, and then obtain the desired result.
nodes.statement_short: Combine cases and take $\tilde\gamma=1$.

nodes.name: Low-frequency estimate of the key term G
nodes.statement: If the matrix $B$ is quasi-stable, the following estimate of $G(t, \xi, \eta)$ holds for $\eta > \beta \gamma$: \begin{displaymath} \|G(t, \xi, \eta)\| \le \frac{C |\xi| e^{\gamma t}}{\eta} \|\exp(H_{11} \cdot)\|_{C^1([0, t])} \log \frac{\eta \delta + \gamma}{\gamma}, \end{displaymath} where $\gamma = \alpha |\xi| + 1$, and the positive constants $C$, $\delta$, $\alpha$ and $\beta$ depend on the matrices $A^j$ and $Q$. Furthermore, if the matrix sets $\mathcal{F}_1$ and $\mathcal{F}_2$ defined in \cref{eq:F1,eq:F2}, respectively, are uniformly quasi-stable, then the following estimate of $G(t, \xi, \eta)$ holds for $\eta > \tilde{\beta}(|\xi| + 1)$: \begin{displaymath} \|G(t, \xi, \eta)\| \le \frac{\tilde{C} |\xi| e^t}{\eta} \log(\eta \tilde{\delta} + 1), \end{displaymath} where the positive constants $\tilde{C}$, $\tilde{\delta}$ and $\tilde{\beta}$ depend on the matrices $A^j$ and $Q$.
nodes.statement_short: $\|G(t,\xi,\eta)\|\lesssim |\xi|e^{\gamma t}\eta^{-1}\log(\cdot)$; uniformly $\lesssim|\xi|e^t\eta^{-1}\log(\eta\tilde\delta+1)$ if $\mathcal{F}_1,\mathcal{F}_2$ are UQS.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4
nodes.statement: This is a direct corollary of \Cref{lemma:gRL}.
nodes.statement_short: Direct corollary of the generalized Riemann-Lebesgue lemma.

nodes.name: Role of the second conclusion of Lemma 3
nodes.statement: The second conclusion in \Cref{lemma:gRL} is crucial for the estimation of $G(t, \xi, \eta)$ that depends linearly on $|\xi|$ and vanishes as $\eta$ tends to infinity. This aspect is essential to derive the corresponding error estimate in \Cref{thm}.

nodes.name: Low-frequency error estimate
nodes.statement: If \cref{eq} is stiffly well-posed, the following convergence holds for each $t > 0$ and $\Xi > 0$: \begin{displaymath} \lim \limits_{\eta \to +\infty} \norm{ \big( \hat{u}(t, \cdot, \eta) - \exp(H_{11} t) \hat{u}_0 \big) \mathbbm{1}_{|\cdot| \le \Xi} }_{L^2} = 0. \end{displaymath} Furthermore, if the matrix sets $\mathcal{F}_1$ and $\mathcal{F}_2$ are uniformly quasi-stable, and the initial data satisfies $U_0 \in H^2$, then there exist positive constants $C$, $\tilde{\delta}$ and $\tilde{\beta}$ dependent on the matrices $A_j$ and $Q$ such that the following estimate holds for each $t > 0$ and $\eta > 2 \tilde{\beta}$: \begin{equation} \norm{ \big( \hat{u}(t, \cdot, \eta) - \exp(H_{11} t) \hat{u}_0 \big) \mathbbm{1}_{|\cdot| \le \Xi(\eta)} }_{L^2} \le \frac{C e^{t}}{\eta} \|U_0\|_{H^2} \log (\eta \tilde{\delta} + 1), \end{equation} where $\Xi(\eta) = \tilde{\beta}^{-1} \eta - 1$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5
nodes.statement_short: Bound the two Mori-Zwanzig remainder terms by $\sup\|G\|$ using Lemma 4 and stiff well-posedness.

nodes.name: G vanishes on bounded frequencies
nodes.statement: By \Cref{lemma:low_frequency_G}, the following convergence holds: \begin{displaymath} \lim \limits_{\eta \to +\infty} \sup_{s \in [0, t]} \sup_{|\xi| \le \Xi} \| G(s, \xi, \eta) \| = 0. \end{displaymath}
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 4 gives $\sup\|G\|\to0$ for $|\xi|\le\Xi$.

nodes.name: Uniform bound on u
nodes.statement: Due to the stiff well-posedness of \cref{eq}, there exists a constant $K_1 > 0$ such that \begin{displaymath} \|{\hat{u}(s, \xi, \eta)}\| \le K_1 \|{\hat{U}_0(\xi)}\|, \end{displaymath} for each $s \ge 0$, $\xi \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and $\eta \ge 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Stiff well-posedness bounds $\hat u$ uniformly.

nodes.name: Conclude convergence
nodes.statement:
Therefore,  egin{multline*} 
orm{  ig( \hat{u}(t, \cdot, \eta) - \exp(H_{11} t) \hat{u}_0  ig) \mathbbm{1}_{|\cdot| \le \Xi} }_{L^2} \ \le 
orm{ G(t, \cdot, \eta) \hat{v}_0 \mathbbm{1}_{|\cdot| \le \Xi} }_{L^2} + \int_0^t 
orm{ G(t-s, \cdot, \eta) H_{21} \hat{u}(s, \cdot, \eta) \mathbbm{1}_{|\cdot| \le \Xi} }_{L^2} \,\mathrm{d} s \ \le \sup_{s \in [0, t]} \sup_{|\xi| \le \Xi} \| G(s, \xi, \eta) \| \cdot  igg( \| \hat{v}_0 \|_{L^2} + t K_1 \sup_{|\xi| \le \Xi} \| H_{21}(\xi, 0) \| \cdot \| \hat{U}_0 \|_{L^2}  igg), \end{multline*} which yields the desired convergence.

nodes.name: Bound each term

nodes.statement_short: Build a contraction on a metric space of slow/fast pairs; the Banach fixed point is the zero-fast-data solution. Key step: the generalized Riemann-Lebesgue lemma makes the fast component $O(\eta^{-1}\log\eta)$, so stiff well-posedness bounds $\exp(H_{11}t)$.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: Let us take fixed $\xi \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and $t > 0$. Our aim is to prove that the matrix exponential $\|\exp(H_{11}(\xi, 0) t)\|$ can be bounded from above by a constant independent of $\xi$ and $t$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $\xi,t$; aim to bound $\exp(H_{11}t)$ uniformly.

nodes.name: Metric space X
nodes.statement: For each $\tilde{u}_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{n - r}$ and $T > 0$, let us define the metric space $X$ as follows, \begin{multline*} X := \Big\{ (\tilde{u}, \tilde{v}) \in C^1([0, T], \mathbb{R}^{n - r}) \times C^0([0, T], \mathbb{R}^r) \,\Big|\, \\ \tilde{u}(0) = \tilde{u}_0, \tilde{v}(0) = 0, \|\tilde{u}\|_{C^1} \le \Lambda_1, \|\tilde{v}\|_{C^0} \le \Lambda_2 \Big\}, \end{multline*} with the metric $\rho$ defined as \begin{displaymath} \rho \big( (\tilde{u}_1, \tilde{v}_1), (\tilde{u}_2, \tilde{v}_2) \big) = \alpha_1 \|\tilde{u}_1 - \tilde{u}_2\|_{C^1} + \alpha_2 \|\tilde{v}_1 - \tilde{v}_2\|_{C^0}, \end{displaymath} where the positive constants $\Lambda_1$, $\Lambda_2$, $\alpha_1$, and $\alpha_2$ are to be determined.
nodes.statement_short: Define the metric space $X$ with weighted metric $\rho$.

nodes.name: Mapping T
nodes.statement: Let us construct the following mapping, \begin{displaymath} \mathcal{T} : (\tilde{u}, \tilde{v}) \in X \mapsto (\mathcal{T}_1(\tilde{u}, \tilde{v}), \mathcal{T}_2(\tilde{u}, \tilde{v})) \in C^1([0, T], \mathbb{R}^{n - r}) \times C^0([0, T], \mathbb{R}^r), \end{displaymath} where \begin{gather*} \mathcal{T}_1(\tilde{u}, \tilde{v})(t) := \exp(H_{11} t) \tilde{u}_0 + \int_0^t \exp(H_{11} (t - s)) H_{12} \tilde{v}(s) \,\mathrm{d} s, \\ \mathcal{T}_2(\tilde{u}, \tilde{v})(t) := \int_0^t \exp(H_{22} (t - s)) H_{21} \tilde{u}(s) \,\mathrm{d} s. \end{gather*}
nodes.statement_short: Define the Duhamel map $\mathcal{T}$.

nodes.name: T maps X into itself
nodes.statement: Let us first prove that $\mathcal{T}(\tilde{u}, \tilde{v}) \in X$ whenever $(\tilde{u}, \tilde{v}) \in X$. By \Cref{lemma:gRL}, one can obtain that \begin{displaymath} \|\mathcal{T}_2(\tilde{u}, \tilde{v})\|_{C^0} \le C \eta^{-1} |\log \eta| \cdot \|\tilde{u}\|_{C^1}, \end{displaymath} for sufficiently large $\eta$. By direct calculation, one can obtain that \begin{displaymath} \|\mathcal{T}_1(\tilde{u}, \tilde{v})\|_{C^1} \le C (\|\tilde{u}_0\| + \|\tilde{v}\|_{C^0}). \end{displaymath} Here the constant $C$ is dependent on $t$, $\xi$, $A_j$ and $Q$, but is independent of $\eta$. As long as \begin{displaymath} C \eta^{-1} |\log \eta| \cdot \Lambda_1 \le \Lambda_2, \quad C (\|u_0\| + \Lambda_2) \le \Lambda_1, \end{displaymath} the mapping $\mathcal{T}$ maps $X$ onto itself.
nodes.statement_short: Show $\mathcal{T}(X)\subset X$.

nodes.name: Fast component small
nodes.statement: By \Cref{lemma:gRL}, one can obtain that \begin{displaymath} \|\mathcal{T}_2(\tilde{u}, \tilde{v})\|_{C^0} \le C \eta^{-1} |\log \eta| \cdot \|\tilde{u}\|_{C^1}, \end{displaymath} for sufficiently large $\eta$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 3 bounds $\mathcal{T}_2$ by $C\eta^{-1}|\log\eta|$.

nodes.name: Slow component bound
nodes.statement: By direct calculation, one can obtain that \begin{displaymath} \|\mathcal{T}_1(\tilde{u}, \tilde{v})\|_{C^1} \le C (\|\tilde{u}_0\| + \|\tilde{v}\|_{C^0}). \end{displaymath} Here the constant $C$ is dependent on $t$, $\xi$, $A_j$ and $Q$, but is independent of $\eta$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\mathcal{T}_1$ directly.

nodes.name: Self-map
nodes.statement: As long as \begin{displaymath} C \eta^{-1} |\log \eta| \cdot \Lambda_1 \le \Lambda_2, \quad C (\|u_0\| + \Lambda_2) \le \Lambda_1, \end{displaymath} the mapping $\mathcal{T}$ maps $X$ onto itself.
nodes.statement_short: Choose constants so $\mathcal{T}$ maps $X$ into itself.

nodes.name: Contraction
nodes.statement: Similarly, note that \begin{multline*} \rho \big( \mathcal{T}(\tilde{u}_1, \tilde{v}_1), \mathcal{T}(\tilde{u}_2, \tilde{v}_2) \big) \\ = \alpha_1 \| \mathcal{T}_1(\tilde{u}_1, \tilde{v}_1) - \mathcal{T}_1(\tilde{u}_2, \tilde{v}_2) \|_{C^1} + \alpha_2 \| \mathcal{T}_2(\tilde{u}_1, \tilde{v}_1) - \mathcal{T}_2(\tilde{u}_2, \tilde{v}_2) \|_{C^0} \\ \le \alpha_1 C \| \tilde{v}_1 - \tilde{v}_2 \|_{C^0} + \alpha_2 C \eta^{-1} |\log \eta| \cdot \| \tilde{u}_1 - \tilde{u}_2 \|_{C^1} \\ \le \frac{1}{2} \alpha_1 \| \tilde{u}_1 - \tilde{u}_2 \|_{C^1} + \frac{1}{2} \alpha_2 \| \tilde{v}_1 - \tilde{v}_2 \|_{C^0} = \frac{1}{2} \rho \big( (\tilde{u}_1, \tilde{v}_1), (\tilde{u}_2, \tilde{v}_2) \big), \end{multline*} as long as \begin{displaymath} \alpha_1 C \le \frac{1}{2} \alpha_2, \quad \alpha_2 C \eta^{-1} |\log \eta| \le \frac{1}{2} \alpha_1. \end{displaymath} At this time, the mapping $\mathcal{T}$ is a contraction mapping on $X$.
nodes.statement_short: Show $\mathcal{T}$ is a 1/2-contraction under constant constraints.

nodes.name: Choice of constants
nodes.statement: For example, one can choose sufficiently large $\eta$ and the constants $\Lambda_1$, $\Lambda_2$, $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$ given by \begin{displaymath} \Lambda_1 = 2 C \norm{\tilde{u}_0}, \quad \Lambda_2 = \norm{\tilde{u}_0}, \quad \alpha_1 = 1, \quad \alpha_2 = 2 C, \end{displaymath} such that all the requirements mentioned previously are satisfied.
nodes.statement_short: Explicit admissible constants.

nodes.name: Picard sequence
nodes.statement: Let us construct the Picard sequence as follows, \begin{gather*} \tilde{u}_0(t) \equiv \tilde{u}_0, \quad \tilde{v}_0(t) \equiv 0, \quad \forall t \in [0, T], \\ (\tilde{u}_{k + 1}, \tilde{v}_{k + 1}) = \mathcal{T}(\tilde{u}_k, \tilde{v}_k), \quad \forall k \in \mathbb{N}. \end{gather*}
nodes.statement_short: Define the Picard iterates.

nodes.name: Banach fixed point
nodes.statement: By the Banach fixed-point theorem, there exists $(\tilde{u}_*, \tilde{v}_*) \in X$ such that \begin{displaymath} \lim\limits_{k \to \infty} \rho \big( (\tilde{u}_k, \tilde{v}_k), (\tilde{u}_*, \tilde{v}_*) \big) = 0. \end{displaymath}
nodes.statement_short: The iterates converge to a fixed point.

nodes.name: Fixed point solves the ODE
nodes.statement: At this time, $(\tilde{u}_*, \tilde{v}_*)$ satisfies the equations \begin{gather*} \tilde{u}_*(t) = \exp(H_{11} t) \tilde{u}_0 + \int_0^t \exp(H_{11} (t - s)) H_{12} \tilde{v}_*(s) \,\mathrm{d} s, \\ \tilde{v}_*(t) = \int_0^t \exp(H_{22} (t - s)) H_{21} \tilde{u}_*(s) \,\mathrm{d} s. \end{gather*} Therefore, $(\tilde{u}_*, \tilde{v}_*)$ is the solution to \begin{gather*} \od{\tilde{u}}{t} = H_{11} \tilde{u} + H_{12} \tilde{v}, \quad \tilde{u}(0) = \tilde{u}_0, \\ \od{\tilde{v}}{t} = H_{21} \tilde{u} + H_{22} \tilde{v}, \quad \tilde{v}(0) = 0. \end{gather*}
nodes.statement_short: The fixed point solves the Fourier ODE with zero fast data.

nodes.name: Stiff well-posedness bound
nodes.statement: According to the definition of stiff well-posedness, there exists a positive constant $\tilde{C}$ independent of $t$, $\xi$ and $\eta$ such that \begin{displaymath} \| \tilde{u}(t) \| \le \tilde{C} \|\tilde{u}_0\|. \end{displaymath}
nodes.statement_short: Stiff well-posedness bounds $\tilde u$.

nodes.name: Integral term small
nodes.statement: Note that there exists a constant $C > 0$ independent of $\eta$ such that \begin{multline*} \nnorm{\int_0^t \exp(H_{11} (t - s)) H_{12} \tilde{v}_*(s) \,\mathrm{d} s} \le C \|{\tilde{v}_*}\|_{C^0} \le C^2 \eta^{-1} |\log \eta| \cdot \|\tilde{u}_*\|_{C^1} \\ \le C^2 \eta^{-1} |\log \eta| \cdot \Lambda_1 = 2 C^3 \eta^{-1} |\log \eta| \cdot \|\tilde{u}_0\|. \end{multline*}
nodes.statement_short: The integral term is $O(\eta^{-1}|\log\eta|)$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: By choosing sufficiently large $\eta$, one can obtain that \begin{displaymath} \|\exp(H_{11} t) \tilde{u}_0\| \le 2 \tilde{C} \|\tilde{u}_0\|, \end{displaymath} where $\tilde{C}$ is independent of $t$ and $\xi$.
nodes.statement_short: Large $\eta$ gives $\|\exp(H_{11}t)\tilde u_0\|\le2\tilde C\|\tilde u_0\|$.

nodes.name: High-frequency estimate
nodes.statement: If \cref{eq} is stiffly well-posed, the following convergence holds for each $t > 0$: \begin{displaymath} \lim_{\Xi \to +\infty} \sup_{t \ge 0} \sup_{\eta \ge 0} \norm{ \big( \hat{u}(t, \cdot, \eta) - \exp(H_{11} t) \hat{u}_0 \big) \mathbbm{1}_{|\cdot| > \Xi} }_{L^2} = 0. \end{displaymath} Furthermore, if the initial data satisfies $U_0 \in H^s$ with $s > 0$, then the following estimate holds: \begin{displaymath} \sup_{t \ge 0} \sup_{\eta \ge 0} \norm{ \big( \hat{u}(t, \cdot, \eta) - \exp(H_{11} t) \hat{u}_0 \big) \mathbbm{1}_{|\cdot| > \Xi} }_{L^2} \le \frac{C}{1 + \Xi^s} \|U_0\|_{H^s}. \end{displaymath}
nodes.statement_short: The high-frequency error vanishes uniformly as the cutoff $\Xi\to\infty$, at rate $\Xi^{-s}$ for $H^s$ data.
