nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 7
nodes.statement: Due to the uniform quasi-stability of the matrix sets $\mathcal{F}_0$ and $\mathcal{F}_1$, there exists a constant $C > 0$ independent of $t$, $\xi$ and $\eta$ such that \begin{displaymath} \|\hat{u}(t, \xi, \eta) - \exp(H_{11} t) \hat{u}_0(\xi)\| \le C \|\hat{U}_0(\xi)\|. \end{displaymath} Therefore, \begin{displaymath} \sup_{t \ge 0} \sup_{\eta \ge 0} \norm{ \big( \hat{u}(t, \cdot, \eta) - \exp(H_{11} t) \hat{u}_0 \big) \mathbbm{1}_{|\cdot| > \Xi} }_{L^2} \le C \| \hat{U}_0 \mathbbm{1}_{|\cdot| > \Xi} \|_{L^2}, \end{displaymath} which yields the desired convergence result. Furthermore, the desired error estimate holds for the initial data $U_0 \in H^s$ with $s > 0$ by noting that \begin{displaymath} \mathbbm{1}_{|\cdot| > \Xi}(\xi) \le \frac{1 + |\xi|^s}{1 + \Xi^s}, \end{displaymath} for each $\xi \in \mathbb{R}^d$.
nodes.statement_short: Uniform quasi-stability of $\mathcal{F}_0$ and $\mathcal{F}_1$ bounds the error by the high-frequency tail of the data.

nodes.name: Pointwise error bound
nodes.statement: Due to the uniform quasi-stability of the matrix sets $\mathcal{F}_0$ and $\mathcal{F}_1$, there exists a constant $C > 0$ independent of $t$, $\xi$ and $\eta$ such that \begin{displaymath} \|\hat{u}(t, \xi, \eta) - \exp(H_{11} t) \hat{u}_0(\xi)\| \le C \|\hat{U}_0(\xi)\|. \end{displaymath}
nodes.statement_short: UQS of $\mathcal{F}_0,\mathcal{F}_1$ bounds the pointwise error.

nodes.name: Convergence
nodes.statement: Therefore, \begin{displaymath} \sup_{t \ge 0} \sup_{\eta \ge 0} \norm{ \big( \hat{u}(t, \cdot, \eta) - \exp(H_{11} t) \hat{u}_0 \big) \mathbbm{1}_{|\cdot| > \Xi} }_{L^2} \le C \| \hat{U}_0 \mathbbm{1}_{|\cdot| > \Xi} \|_{L^2}, \end{displaymath} which yields the desired convergence result.
nodes.statement_short: Error bounded by the data's tail.

nodes.name: Rate
nodes.statement: Furthermore, the desired error estimate holds for the initial data $U_0 \in H^s$ with $s > 0$ by noting that \begin{displaymath} \mathbbm{1}_{|\cdot| > \Xi}(\xi) \le \frac{1 + |\xi|^s}{1 + \Xi^s}, \end{displaymath} for each $\xi \in \mathbb{R}^d$.
nodes.statement_short: Rate from $\mathbb{1}_{|\xi|>\Xi}\le(1+|\xi|^s)/(1+\Xi^s)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Split frequencies at $\Xi$: the high-frequency error is small by Lemma 7, the low-frequency error by Lemma 5; strong hyperbolicity comes from Lemma 6.

nodes.name: Strong hyperbolicity
nodes.statement: By \Cref{lemma:UQS_of_F1}, the stiff well-posedness of \cref{eq} ensures the strong hyperbolicity of reduced systems presented in \cref{eq:reduced}.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 6 gives strong hyperbolicity of the reduced system.

nodes.name: High-frequency cutoff
nodes.statement: Given arbitrary $\mu > 0$ and $t > 0$, let us take a sufficiently large $\Xi > 0$ such that \begin{displaymath} \sup_{\eta \ge 0} \norm{ \big( \hat{u}(t, \cdot, \eta) - \exp(H_{11} t) \hat{u}_0 \big) \mathbbm{1}_{|\cdot| > \Xi} }_{L^2} < \frac{1}{2} \mu, \end{displaymath} according to \Cref{lemma:high_frequency}.
nodes.statement_short: Choose $\Xi$ by Lemma 7.

nodes.name: Low-frequency bound
nodes.statement: By \Cref{lemma:low_frequency}, there exists a constant $\Theta > 0$ such that the following inequality holds for each $\eta > \Theta$: \begin{displaymath} \norm{ \big( \hat{u}(t, \cdot, \eta) - \exp(H_{11} t) \hat{u}_0 \big) \mathbbm{1}_{|\cdot| \le \Xi} }_{L^2} < \frac{1}{2} \mu. \end{displaymath}
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 5 bounds the low-frequency error.

nodes.name: Convergence
nodes.statement: At this time, one can obtain that \begin{displaymath} \norm{ \big( \hat{u}(t, \cdot, \eta) - \exp(H_{11} t) \hat{u}_0 \big) }_{L^2} < \mu, \end{displaymath} which yields the desired convergence.
nodes.statement_short: Total error $<\mu$.

nodes.name: Low-frequency rate
nodes.statement: Furthermore, if the matrix set $\mathcal{F}_2$ is uniformly quasi-stable and the initial data satisfies $U_0 \in H^2$, then the error estimate at the low-frequency region with the frequency cutoff $\Xi(\eta) = \tilde{\beta}^{-1} \eta - 1$ can be given by \cref{eq:low_frequency_error} in \Cref{lemma:low_frequency}.
nodes.statement_short: Use (19) with cutoff $\Xi(\eta)$.

nodes.name: High-frequency rate and conclusion
nodes.statement: At the high-frequency region, the error can be bounded by \begin{displaymath} \norm{ \big( \hat{u}(t, \cdot, \eta) - \exp(H_{11} t) \hat{u}_0 \big) \mathbbm{1}_{|\cdot| > \Xi(\eta)} }_{L^2} \le \frac{C}{1 + \Xi(\eta)^2} \|U_0\|_{H^2}. \end{displaymath} Combining the high- and low-frequency estimates, we complete the proof of this theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the tail by $C(1+\Xi(\eta)^2)^{-1}$ and combine.

nodes.name: K(M) measures quasi-stability
nodes.statement: Let $M \in \mathbb{C}^{n \times n}$. The matrix $M$ is quasi-stable, if and only if $\mathcal{K}(M) < + \infty$.
nodes.statement_short: $M$ is quasi-stable iff $\mathcal{K}(M)<\infty$.
assumptions: Let $M \in \mathbb{C}^{n \times n}$.
conclusions: The matrix $M$ is quasi-stable, if and only if $\mathcal{K}(M) < + \infty$.

nodes.name: Spectrum in closed left half-plane
nodes.statement: First, we assume that the matrix $M$ is quasi-stable. \Cref{lemma:QS_character} yields that the spectrum $\sigma(M)$ is a subset of the closed left half-plane $\mathbb{H}^{\mathrm{c}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 1 places the spectrum in $\mathbb{H}^c$.

nodes.name: Jordan form
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the Jordan matrix.

nodes.name: Reduce to Jordan blocks
nodes.statement: To estimate $\norm{(z I - J)^{-1}}$, it suffices to estimate the resolvent of each Jordan block. Let \begin{displaymath} J_r = \begin{pmatrix} \lambda_r & 1 & & \\ & \ddots & \ddots & \\ & & \ddots & 1 \\ & & & \lambda_r \end{pmatrix} = \lambda_r I + N \in \mathbb{C}^{k \times k} \end{displaymath} be an arbitrary Jordan block of $J$.
nodes.statement_short: Suffices to estimate each Jordan block.

nodes.name: Block resolvent expansion
nodes.statement: By direct calculation, one has that \begin{equation} (z I - J_r)^{-1} = \sum_{j = 0}^{k - 1} (z - \lambda_r)^{-(j + 1)} N^j, \quad z \in \mathbb{H}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Finite Neumann expansion of the block resolvent.

nodes.name: Stable eigenvalue
nodes.statement_short: Bound the block resolvent for $\Re\lambda_r<0$.

nodes.name: Imaginary eigenvalue
nodes.statement: If $\Re(\lambda_r) = 0$, then \Cref{lemma:QS_character} yields that the order of $J_r$ is $k = 1$, and thus \begin{displaymath} \norm{(z I - J_r)^{-1}} = |z - \lambda_r|^{-1} \le \max_{\lambda \in \sigma(M) \setminus \mathbb{H}} |z - \lambda|^{-1}, \quad z \in \mathbb{H}. \end{displaymath}
nodes.statement_short: Semi-simple case is trivial.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Therefore, we obtain that $\mathcal{K}(M) < + \infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Hence $\mathcal{K}(M)<\infty$.

nodes.name: Finite K implies quasi-stable
nodes.statement_short: Prove the converse by contradiction.

nodes.name: Largest Jordan block
nodes.statement: Conversely, we assume that $\mathcal{K}(M) < + \infty$. Let $\lambda_r$ be an arbitrary eigenvalue of $M$, and $J_r \in \mathbb{C}^{k \times k}$ be the largest Jordan block corresponding to $\lambda_r$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick an eigenvalue and its largest Jordan block.

nodes.name: Resolvent blow-up rate
nodes.statement: By \cref{equ:resolventJr}, one can obtain that \begin{displaymath} \norm{(z I - M)^{-1}} \sim |z - \lambda_r|^{-k}, \quad \text{ as } z \rightarrow \lambda_r. \end{displaymath}
nodes.statement_short: Resolvent blows up like $|z-\lambda_r|^{-k}$.

nodes.name: Unstable eigenvalue
nodes.statement: If $\Re(\lambda_r) > 0$, then \begin{displaymath} \frac{\norm{(z I - M)^{-1}}} {\max_{\lambda \in \sigma(M) \setminus \mathbb{H}} |z - \lambda|^{-1}} \sim |z - \lambda_r|^{-k}, \quad \text{ as } z \rightarrow \lambda_r. \end{displaymath}
nodes.statement_short: Ratio unbounded.

nodes.name: Non-semi-simple imaginary eigenvalue
nodes.statement: If $\Re(\lambda_r) = 0$ and $k > 1$, then \begin{displaymath} \frac{\norm{(z I - M)^{-1}}} {\max_{\lambda \in \sigma(M) \setminus \mathbb{H}} |z - \lambda|^{-1}} \sim |z - \lambda_r|^{- k + 1}, \quad \text{ as } z \rightarrow \lambda_r. \end{displaymath}
nodes.statement_short: Ratio unbounded.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Both cases yield a contradiction, and then the quasi-stability of the matrix $M$ follows from \Cref{lemma:QS_character}.
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction; Lemma 1 gives quasi-stability.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 9
nodes.statement_short: Factor $A$ into elementary rank-one updates whose inverses are explicit, and bound each factor's norm by $n\alpha$.

nodes.name: Column partition
nodes.statement: Let the column partitioning of the strictly upper triangular component of $A$ be \begin{displaymath} U := A - I = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & u_2 & \cdots & u_n \end{pmatrix}. \end{displaymath} Denote the $i$th column of the identity matrix $I$ as $e_i$. It is clear that $e_i^\top u_j = 0$ for $2 \le j \le i \le n$.
nodes.statement_short: Write $A-I$ by columns and note $e_i^\top u_j=0$.

nodes.name: Factorization of A and its inverse
nodes.statement: Therefore, one can obtain that \begin{multline*} A = I + u_n e_n^\top + u_{n - 1} e_{n - 1}^\top + \ldots + u_2 e_2^\top \\ = \left( I + u_n e_n^\top \right) \left( I + u_{n - 1} e_{n - 1}^\top \right) \ldots \left( I + u_2 e_2^\top \right), \end{multline*} and that \begin{displaymath} I = \left( I + u_j e_j^\top \right) \left( I - u_j e_j^\top \right), \quad \text{ for } j = 2, 3, \ldots, n, \end{displaymath} which yields that \begin{displaymath} A^{-1} = \left( I - u_2 e_2^\top \right) \left( I - u_3 e_3^\top \right) \ldots \left( I - u_n e_n^\top \right). \end{displaymath}
nodes.statement_short: Factor $A$ and invert each factor.

nodes.name: Factor norm bound
nodes.statement_short: Each factor has norm at most $n\alpha$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement_short: Multiply the $n-1$ bounds.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: Sufficiency via Lemma 8 and Kreiss's resolvent condition; necessity via the Kreiss triangular form, splitting the resolvent into a diagonal part and a unit upper triangular factor bounded by Lemma 9.

nodes.name: Sufficiency
nodes.statement: First, we assume that the set of matrices $\mathcal{F}$ satisfies \cref{eq:uniformKM}. By \Cref{lemma:QS_KM}, each matrix in $\mathcal{F}$ is quasi-stable. For each $M \in \mathcal{F}$, $z \in \mathbb{H}$, and $\lambda \in \sigma(M) = \sigma(M) \setminus \mathbb{H}$, one has that \begin{displaymath} 0 < \Re(z) \le \Re(z - \lambda) \le |z - \lambda|, \end{displaymath} which yields that \begin{multline*} \sup_{M \in \mathcal{F}} \sup_{z \in \mathbb{H}} \left( \Re(z) \cdot \norm{(z I - M)^{-1}} \right) \\ \le \sup_{M \in \mathcal{F}} \sup_{z \in \mathbb{H}} \frac{\norm{(z I - M)^{-1}}} {\max_{\lambda \in \sigma(M) \setminus \mathbb{H}} |z - \lambda|^{-1}} = \sup_{M \in \mathcal{F}} \mathcal{K}(M) < + \infty. \end{multline*} Therefore, the set of matrices $\mathcal{F}$ is uniformly quasi-stable thanks to \Cref{thm:KMT}.
nodes.statement_short: Bounded $\mathcal{K}$ implies UQS.
